knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of fixed block bandwidth under nonlocal horizon coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a constraint row contains nonzero coefficients in stage blocks \(i\) and \(j\), where \(|i-j|\) grows with \(N\). Its multiplier \(\lambda_c\) is adjacent in the KKT sparsity graph to both distant blocks. Under the natural temporal ordering, this creates a coupling span that grows with the horizon, so the fixed-band stagewise KKT property is lost. Eliminating \(\lambda_c\) may create direct fill between all stage blocks in that row. A reformulation with auxiliary states can recover local structure only when the long-range quantity admits an exact finite-dimensional stagewise recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint spanning increasingly distant stages destroys fixed temporal bandwidth unless an exact auxiliary-state recursion localizes it.

children.title: Riccati Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Sparse optimal-control QP structures compatible with Riccati-style linear algebra.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense arithmetic and storage scaling for the unconstrained finite-horizon Riccati interface with uniformly bounded stage dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\dim x_k\le n_x\) and \(\dim u_k\le n_u\), and suppose every control-curvature matrix factored in the backward recursion is nonsingular. A dense backward Riccati sweep and forward recovery require \(O\!\left(N(n_x+n_u)^3\right)\) arithmetic operations. Retaining all feedback gains and value matrices requires \(O\!\left(N(n_x^2+n_xn_u)\right)\) storage; the backward sweep alone has horizon-independent working storage if stage data can be accessed in reverse order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed state and input dimensions, dense Riccati recursion has linear arithmetic growth in the horizon; retaining all stage factors also requires linear storage.
assumptions_latex: Every control-curvature matrix factored during the backward sweep is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{work}=O\!\left(N(n_x+n_u)^3\right),\qquad \operatorname{stored\ stage\ factors}=O\!\left(N(n_x^2+n_xn_u)\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Horizon Complexity of Riccati Recursion

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(P_N=Q_N\). For \(k=N-1,\ldots,0\), define \[G_k=R_k+B_k^{\mathsf T}P_{k+1}B_k,\qquad K_k=-G_k^{-1}B_k^{\mathsf T}P_{k+1}A_k,\] \[P_k=Q_k+A_k^{\mathsf T}P_{k+1}A_k-A_k^{\mathsf T}P_{k+1}B_kG_k^{-1}B_k^{\mathsf T}P_{k+1}A_k.\] Since \(R_k\succ0\), every \(G_k\succ0\). Forward propagation with \(u_k=K_kx_k\) yields the optimizer. These recursions are the stagewise Schur-complement elimination of the sparse dynamics-constrained KKT system; active general inequalities require a different or augmented interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riccati recursion is the stagewise Schur-complement factorization of the unconstrained finite-horizon LQ KKT system.

children.title: Sparse-KKT Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Sparse optimal-control QP structures exposed through general KKT-system interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-KKT Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT matrix exposed by an uncondensed finite-horizon linear MPC model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For horizon variables \(z=(x_1,u_0,\ldots,x_N,u_{N-1})\), let \(H\succeq0\) be stage-block diagonal and let \(Az=b\) encode \(x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k+d_k\). The equality-constrained Newton system has the interface
\[\begin{pmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta z\\\Delta\lambda\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}r_d\\r_p\end{pmatrix}.\]
Under a stagewise ordering, \(A\) is block bidiagonal and the displayed KKT matrix has block bandwidth independent of the horizon. Adding active or barrier-treated stage-local inequalities augments only corresponding stage blocks, so the sparse optimal-control adjacency is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uncondensed MPC Newton equations form a block-banded saddle-point system whose bandwidth does not grow with the prediction horizon.
assumptions_latex: The objective Hessian and inequality contributions are stage-local.
Variables and multipliers are ordered by stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT interface is block sparse with horizon-independent block bandwidth.

notation.meaning: Hessian of the stagewise quadratic objective

children.title: Linear-Algebra Interface Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions favoring specialized recursion or general sparse factorization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interface Selection Is Not a Strict Dichotomy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrects the boundary between classical Riccati pivots and alternative linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Failure or poor conditioning of a classical reduced control pivot \(G_k\) invalidates that unmodified pivot sequence, but does not force one unique alternative interface. Depending on rank, definiteness, coupling, and available structure, admissible responses can include symmetric pivoting, consistent regularization, alternative elimination orderings, constraint-aware or generalized Riccati recursions, null-space reduction, and iterative saddle-point methods. Limited nonlocal coupling may also be represented by state augmentation or another structured extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unusable classical Riccati pivot invalidates that recursion, not every Riccati-like method; several structured and general alternatives may remain.
assumptions_latex: Classical Riccati recursion denotes the specified unregularized stagewise pivot sequence.
Any alternative method preserves or consistently regularizes the original KKT equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_k\text{ unusable}\Longrightarrow\text{the classical pivot sequence fails},\quad\text{not a unique mandatory solver class}.

notation.meaning: classical reduced control pivot at stage k

knowledge_statements.title: Interface Selection Is Not a Strict Dichotomy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Riccati Recursion as Structured KKT Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common algebraic basis of Riccati and assembled sparse-KKT interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stage-ordered linear-quadratic optimal-control KKT system with adjacent-stage dynamics, backward Riccati recursion is block elimination in temporal order: stage elimination forms successive Schur complements, and the forward sweep recovers eliminated variables. An assembled sparse-KKT factorization applies elimination to the same saddle-point equations but may use different ordering, pivoting, and regularization. When both perform exact admissible eliminations of the same nonsingular KKT system, they recover the same primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riccati recursion and sparse-KKT factorization solve the same KKT equations through different elimination interfaces.
assumptions_latex: Both interfaces represent the same quadratic model and linear constraints.
Every elimination used by each method is admissible and exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{\mathrm{Riccati}}=z_{\mathrm{KKT}}\quad\text{when both exact interfaces solve the same nonsingular KKT system}.
knowledge_statements.title: Riccati Recursion as Structured KKT Elimination
Linear-Algebra Interface Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions selecting Riccati elimination or general sparse-indefinite KKT linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the stagewise KKT system of a linear-quadratic horizon problem. A Riccati interface is admissible when successive elimination of each control block produces nonsingular reduced control pivots \(G_k\), permitting backward Schur-complement recursion followed by forward recovery. If some required \(G_k\) is singular or numerically unacceptable, or if nonlocal constraints destroy the stage chain, the interface must instead expose the assembled sparse symmetric-indefinite KKT matrix to a pivoted sparse factorization or an iterative saddle-point solver. Thus the interface regime is determined by pivot admissibility and preservation of the stagewise chain, not by convexity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Riccati recursion applies when stagewise control pivots are usable and the chain structure survives; otherwise the model requires a general sparse KKT solver.
assumptions_latex: The horizon model has a twice-differentiable quadratic objective and linear constraints.
A stagewise variable ordering is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Usable stage pivots and chain structure select Riccati recursion; their failure selects a general sparse-KKT interface.

notation.meaning: reduced control pivot at stage k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits, but failure of a reduced control pivot does not by itself force the stated solver choices; generalized Riccati, regularization, or alternative eliminations may remain possible. An authoritative source is needed to delimit the regimes.

children.title: State-Elimination Forms
children.top_down_role: Condensed MPC representations retaining inputs while eliminating predicted states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between feasible condensed inputs and sparse trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X(U)=\mathcal A x_0+\mathcal B U+\mathcal d\) be the unique solution of the explicit affine horizon dynamics for fixed \(x_0\). Then \[U\mapsto (X(U),U)\] is a bijection from the feasible set of the exactly condensed QP onto the feasible set of the original trajectory QP. Corresponding points have identical objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact state elimination neither loses nor creates feasible trajectories: every feasible condensed input has one recoverable trajectory with the same objective value.
assumptions_latex: Every occurrence of an eliminated state is substituted in the objective and constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Condensed minimizers lift exactly to trajectory-form minimizers through \(X(U)\).

notation.meaning: unique predicted trajectory recovered from U

knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory-Recovery Bijection
State-Elimination Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full state elimination for an affine, time-varying linear MPC prediction model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k+d_k\), with fixed \(x_0\), and stack \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) and \(U=(u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1})\). Repeated substitution gives
\[X=\mathcal A x_0+\mathcal B U+\mathcal d,\]
where the block in row \(i\), column \(j\) of \(\mathcal B\) is zero for \(j\ge i\) and equals \(A_{i-1}A_{i-2}\cdots A_{j+1}B_j\) for \(j<i\), with an empty product interpreted as the identity. Substitution into the cost and constraints yields a QP whose only trajectory decision vector is \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated dynamics substitution expresses every predicted state affinely in the initial state and stacked controls, producing a control-only condensed QP.
assumptions_latex: All prediction dynamics are affine and equality constrained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state trajectory satisfies \(X=\mathcal A x_0+\mathcal B U+\mathcal d\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The state-elimination representation and indexing are coherent, but the record provides no inspectable citation for the MPC condensation formula.

children.title: Dense Horizon Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cross-stage quadratic and constraint coupling introduced by state elimination.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Causal Coupling of Condensed Path Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-stage affine-constraint coupling produced by eliminating predicted states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stage constraints \(G_kx_k+E_ku_k\le r_k\) and predictions \(x_k=a_k+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}S_{kj}u_j\), exact substitution gives \[\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}G_kS_{kj}u_j+E_ku_k\le r_k-G_ka_k.\] Thus the row for stage \(k\) can couple every earlier control that influences \(x_k\), but no later control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A condensed path-constraint row may couple the current control with all causally relevant earlier controls, but never with future controls.
assumptions_latex: The prediction dynamics and path constraints are affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condensed path-constraint matrix has causal cross-stage coupling.

notation.meaning: map from the control at stage j to the state at stage k

knowledge_statements.title: Causal Coupling of Condensed Path Constraints
Dense Horizon Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-stage control coupling created by full state elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the state cost is \(\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{N}x_k^{\mathsf T}Q_kx_k\) and the input cost is \(\frac12\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}u_k^{\mathsf T}R_ku_k\). With \(X=\mathcal A x_0+\mathcal B U+\mathcal d\), the condensed Hessian is
\[H_c=\mathcal B^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Q\mathcal B+\mathcal R.\]
Its \((i,j)\) input block equals \(\delta_{ij}R_i+\sum_{k>\max\{i,j\}}\mathcal B_{ki}^{\mathsf T}Q_k\mathcal B_{kj}\). Hence two controls become coupled whenever both influence a later state carrying a nonzero quadratic weight; absent special cancellations or finite-memory dynamics, \(H_c\) is block dense across the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condensation couples controls that influence a common future weighted state, so the control Hessian is generally dense across time.
assumptions_latex: The states are eliminated using the affine prediction map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condensed Hessian is \(H_c=\mathcal B^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Q\mathcal B+\mathcal R\) and is generally block dense.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condensed-Hessian formula and qualified density claim fit this property leaf, but no source or locator supports them.

children.title: Condensation Fill-In Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem structures determining the extent and impact of densification after elimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural effect of eliminating states in finite groups rather than across the complete MPC horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the horizon into contiguous groups and eliminate only states internal to each group, retaining boundary states. This partial condensation produces dense coupling within each group but preserves coupling through the retained boundaries between groups. Group size one recovers the uncondensed sparse trajectory form, while one horizon-length group recovers full condensation. Intermediate group sizes interpolate between decision dimension and fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial condensation trades fewer retained states for denser within-group coupling; its endpoint cases are the sparse uncondensed and fully condensed formulations.
assumptions_latex: The linear MPC dynamics permit exact elimination of internal group states
Groups are contiguous along the horizon
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Increasing condensation-group size generally reduces retained state variables while enlarging dense within-group blocks.

notation.meaning: a contiguous condensation group of horizon stages

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Condensation Fill Tradeoff

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Storage Boundary for Condensed Fill Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizon scaling of explicit condensed-Hessian storage under bounded bandwidth and horizon-wide fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(N\) control blocks of fixed dimension \(m\), a condensed Hessian with fixed block half-bandwidth \(w\) requires \(O(Nwm^2)\) explicit block storage, whereas horizon-wide block fill requires \(O(N^2m^2)\). Thus fixed finite prediction memory gives storage linear in the horizon, while persistent dense coupling gives quadratic horizon storage. Factorization costs depend additionally on numerical ordering and block structure and are not determined by fill classification alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed block bandwidth gives linear-horizon Hessian storage; horizon-wide fill gives quadratic-horizon storage.
assumptions_latex: There are \(N\) control blocks of fixed dimension \(m\)
The Hessian is stored explicitly by nonzero blocks
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{storage}=O(Nwm^2)\) for block bandwidth \(w\), versus \(O(N^2m^2)\) for horizon-wide fill.
knowledge_statements.title: Storage Boundary for Condensed Fill Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise criterion distinguishing absent, bounded-range, and horizon-wide coupling after MPC state elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With block-diagonal state and input weights, let \(\mathcal B_{ki}\) map control block \(u_i\) to predicted state \(x_k\). The condensed Hessian blocks satisfy \[(H_c)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}R_i+\sum_{k>\max\{i,j\}}\mathcal B_{ki}^{\mathsf T}Q_k\mathcal B_{kj}.\] Hence an off-diagonal block is absent exactly when the displayed sum is zero. If \(\mathcal B_{ki}=0\) whenever \(k-i>L\), then \((H_c)_{ij}=0\) whenever \(|i-j|\ge L\), so the block half-bandwidth is at most \(L-1\). If arbitrarily separated controls jointly affect weighted future states and the corresponding cross-term sums do not cancel, nonzero blocks occur arbitrarily far from the diagonal, producing horizon-wide fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite control-to-state memory bounds condensed Hessian bandwidth; persistent shared influence with noncancelling cross terms produces horizon-wide coupling.
assumptions_latex: State and input weights are block diagonal by stage
The condensed state map is obtained by exact linear-dynamics elimination
The horizon-wide conclusion includes the stated noncancellation condition
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite influence length \(L\) implies block half-bandwidth at most \(L-1\); persistent noncancelling shared influence permits horizon-wide fill.

notation.meaning: map from control block i to predicted state k
condensed Hessian block coupling controls i and j

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Condensed-Hessian Fill Criterion
Condensation Fill-In Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion distinguishing band-limited from horizon-wide condensed Hessian fill-in.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For condensed Hessian blocks
\[(H_c)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}R_i+\sum_{k>\max\{i,j\}}\mathcal B_{ki}^{\mathsf T}Q_k\mathcal B_{kj},\]
a pair \((i,j)\) has no condensation fill-in exactly when the displayed sum is zero. If \(\mathcal B_{ki}=0\) whenever \(k-i>L\), then \((H_c)_{ij}=0\) for \(|i-j|\ge L\), apart from input-cost blocks, and the condensed Hessian has bounded block bandwidth. If controls at arbitrarily separated stages jointly affect weighted future states and their summed cross terms do not cancel, nonzero blocks occur arbitrarily far from the diagonal, giving horizon-wide fill-in.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite prediction memory limits condensed fill-in; persistent shared influence on weighted future states creates horizon-wide coupling.
assumptions_latex: The stage state and input weights are block diagonal.
The condensed state map \(\mathcal B\) is defined by exact dynamics elimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-dependent dense-solver data for repeated MPC QPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the dynamics, weights, horizon, and constraint matrices are fixed while only \(x_0\) varies, the condensed QP can be written \[\min_U\ \tfrac12U^{\mathsf T}H_cU+(g_0+G_xx_0)^{\mathsf T}U\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \ell_0+L_xx_0\le C_cU\le u_0+R_xx_0.\] Thus \(H_c,C_c\) and the affine parameter maps can be assembled offline, while each online instance updates only vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed model matrices, the dense Hessian and constraint matrix can be precomputed; the measured initial state changes only affine vectors.
assumptions_latex: Model matrices, horizon, weights, and constraint coefficient matrices are fixed.
The initial state enters through the affine prediction map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only the dense objective and bound vectors require online affine evaluation in \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Offline-Online Dense Data Separation
Dense QP Solver Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical dense-solver data exported by a fully condensed MPC formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
After eliminating all predicted states, a dense QP solver may be given
\[\min_{U\in\mathbb R^{Nn_u}}\ \frac12U^{\mathsf T}H_cU+g_c^{\mathsf T}U\quad\text{subject to}\quad \ell_c\le C_cU\le u_c.\]
Here \(H_c=\mathcal B^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Q\mathcal B+\mathcal R\), while \(g_c\), \(C_c\), \(\ell_c\), and \(u_c\) are obtained by substituting the affine state prediction into the original objective and bounds. The interface is valid for a convex dense QP solver when \(H_c\succeq0\); equalities are represented by coincident lower and upper bounds or by a separate equality matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully condensed MPC model exports a control-only convex QP with a generally dense Hessian and substituted linear constraints.
assumptions_latex: All predicted states have been eliminated exactly.
The original cost is convex quadratic and all constraints are linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solver interface is a control-only QP with \(H_c\succeq0\) and affine two-sided constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Post-solve recovery of predicted states from the dense control vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a condensed solution \(U^\star\), reconstruct \(x_{k+1}^\star=A_kx_k^\star+B_ku_k^\star+d_k\) from the measured \(x_0\). Under exact state substitution, a feasible optimal \(U^\star\) thereby yields a feasible optimal trajectory-form pair \((X^\star,U^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward simulation reconstructs predicted states from the dense solver's control output.
assumptions_latex: The dense QP was obtained by exact state substitution.
\(U^\star\) is a feasible optimal condensed solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X^\star,U^\star)\) is feasible and optimal for the trajectory-form QP.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness and Recovery of Block Condensation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a sparse horizon QP and its partially condensed macro-stage QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume every eliminated internal state is uniquely determined by the retained block-entry state and within-block controls through affine dynamics. Exact substitution then gives a bijection between feasible original trajectories and feasible partially condensed variables. Corresponding points have equal objective values; consequently both QPs have the same optimal value, every condensed optimizer reconstructs an original optimizer by within-block forward simulation, and the projection of every original optimizer is condensed-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial condensation is exact elimination: feasible trajectories, objective values, and optimizers correspond, with internal states recovered by forward simulation.
assumptions_latex: Dynamics determine each successor state uniquely and affinely.
Every occurrence of an eliminated state in the objective and constraints is substituted exactly.
The initial state is fixed data or retained explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_{\mathrm{pc}}=p_{\mathrm{sparse}},\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}P_{\mathrm{pc}}\leftrightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}P_{\mathrm{sparse}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness and Recovery of Block Condensation
Block-Condensing Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial condensation over a fixed partition of the MPC horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose boundaries \(0=b_0<b_1<\cdots<b_M=N\), retain the boundary states \(X_j=x_{b_j}\), and stack the controls within block \(j\) as \(V_j=(u_{b_j},\ldots,u_{b_{j+1}-1})\). Eliminating only the internal states gives
\[X_{j+1}=\Phi_jX_j+\Gamma_jV_j+\eta_j,\qquad j=0,\ldots,M-1,\]
where \(\Phi_j=A_{b_{j+1}-1}\cdots A_{b_j}\), and \(\Gamma_j\) contains the corresponding within-block transition products multiplying each control. Substitution condenses each block cost and constraint while preserving a chain of \(M\) macro-stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial condensation eliminates states inside horizon blocks while retaining boundary states, producing a shorter optimal-control chain with blockwise dense data.
assumptions_latex: The horizon dynamics are affine and linear in state and control.
The block boundaries form a partition of \(\{0,\ldots,N\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Internal-state elimination produces the macro-dynamics \(X_{j+1}=\Phi_jX_j+\Gamma_jV_j+\eta_j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The block-condensing representation is coherent and matches the leaf, but the macro-dynamics construction is unsupported by a cited partial-condensing source.

children.title: Dimension-Reduction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Partial-condensing choices organized by the resulting number of optimization variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Reduction Is Not Complexity Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits the interpretation of partial-condensing decision counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reduction from \(Nn_x+Nn_u\) to \(Mn_x+Nn_u\) counts explicit primal coordinates only. It does not imply a proportional reduction in arithmetic time or memory: eliminating internal states may densify block Hessians and constraint matrices, enlarge frontal blocks, or change factorization fill. Consequently partitions with the same \(M\) can have different computational costs when their block lengths, local constraints, orderings, or numerical linear-algebra implementations differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smaller explicit decision vector does not by itself guarantee less solution time or memory because condensation can create denser algebra.
assumptions_latex: Dimension means the number of explicitly retained primal coordinates.
Computational cost is assessed separately from coordinate count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(P_1)\le d(P_2)\centernot\Rightarrow\operatorname{cost}(P_1)\le\operatorname{cost}(P_2).

notation.meaning: explicit primal dimension under partition P

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Reduction Is Not Complexity Reduction
Dimension-Reduction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-dimension reduction under partial condensation with fixed initial state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a horizon of \(N\) stages have state dimension \(n_x\), input dimension \(n_u\), and \(M\) condensing blocks. With fixed \(x_0\), the sparse formulation contains \(Nn_x+Nn_u\) trajectory decision coordinates. Retaining only the \(M\) block-end states and all controls gives \(Mn_x+Nn_u\) coordinates and eliminates exactly \((N-M)n_x\) state coordinates. Thus larger blocks, equivalently smaller \(M\), produce greater state-dimension reduction; retaining every stage corresponds to \(M=N\), whereas eliminating every predicted state leaves \(Nn_u\) coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With M retained block-end states, partial condensation removes exactly (N−M) state blocks while leaving all N control blocks.
assumptions_latex: The initial state is data rather than a decision variable.
All state and control dimensions are constant across stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partial condensation reduces the decision dimension from \(Nn_x+Nn_u\) to \(Mn_x+Nn_u\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimension count is consistent when the fixed initial state is excluded and all block-end states are retained, but no cited source supports the stated partial-condensing regime.

children.title: Sparsity-Retention Regimes
children.top_down_role: Partial-condensing choices organized by preservation of block or stagewise sparsity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition under which the macro-stage path graph is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the macro-stage interaction graph contain an edge \(i\sim j\) whenever an objective or constraint block jointly contains variables from macro-stages \(i\) and \(j\). Under macro-stage ordering, path structure is retained only when all edges join equal or adjacent stages. Any structural coupling with \(|i-j|>1\) adds a nonpath edge; families of horizon-wide couplings can make bandwidth and factor fill grow with \(M\), even when every condensing block has bounded length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded block length does not preserve path sparsity when costs or constraints couple nonadjacent macro-stages.
assumptions_latex: Structural nonzeros are assessed before accidental numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(i,j),\ |i-j|>1,\ i\sim j\Longrightarrow\text{the macro-stage interaction graph is not a path}.

notation.meaning: structural coupling between macro-stages i and j

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlocal-Coupling Boundary for Macro-Stage Sparsity
Sparsity-Retention Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Macro-stage sparsity retained by bounded-size partial-condensing blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition into \(M\) blocks, partial condensation replaces the original stage chain by the macro-dynamics \(X_{j+1}=\Phi_jX_j+\Gamma_jV_j+\eta_j\). If costs and constraints do not connect nonadjacent blocks, the macro-stage KKT graph remains a path: each dynamics row touches only \((X_j,V_j,X_{j+1})\). Consequently its block bandwidth is independent of \(M\). Condensation may make the matrices within each macro-stage dense; if the maximum block length \(L_{\max}\) is bounded independently of \(N\), those dense blocks have uniformly bounded dimension. Unbounded block lengths retain the path graph but create increasingly large dense frontal blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial condensation preserves a path-structured KKT graph, while block length controls the size of its dense macro-stage blocks.
assumptions_latex: All costs and constraints are local to one block or an adjacent boundary state.
The variables and multipliers are ordered by macro-stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The macro-KKT graph has horizon-independent block bandwidth; uniformly bounded block lengths also bound block size.

notation.meaning: maximum number of original stages in one block

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the sparsity-retention leaf, but the macro-KKT bandwidth and frontal-block claims require an authoritative partial-condensing linear-algebra source.

children.title: Memory-Footprint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Partial-condensing choices organized by matrix storage and factorization workspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage bound with explicit local-dimension and factorization assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let block \(j\) contain \(L_j\) controls, let \(w_j=n_x+L_jn_u\) be its primal macro-stage dimension, and let \(q_j\) bound its local constraint and multiplier dimension. If local data are stored as dense blocks, their storage is \(O(\sum_j(w_j+q_j)^2)\). If the macro-stage KKT graph is a path and block elimination uses admissible local pivots without horizon-growing pivot fill, factor storage has the same structural order. Thus, when \(n_x,n_u,L_{\max}\), and \(q_{\max}\) are independent of \(N\), storage is \(O(M)\). A fully condensed dense control Hessian can require \(O((Nn_u)^2)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded macro-stage and local-constraint dimensions give linear structural storage in the number of macro-stages, subject to path-preserving factorization assumptions.
assumptions_latex: Macro-stage data are stored as dense local blocks.
\(q_j\) includes all local constraint and multiplier dimensions relevant to stored KKT blocks.
The macro-stage graph is a path under the chosen ordering.
Pivoting and regularization do not introduce horizon-growing fill.
Only asymptotic scalar storage is counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{storage}=O\!\left(\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}(w_j+q_j)^2\right)=O(M)\quad\text{under uniform bounds}.

notation.meaning: maximum block length and local constraint dimension

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Bounded-Block Storage Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requirements for meaningful memory comparisons between condensing partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A memory footprint is meaningful only after specifying stored primal, constraint, and multiplier blocks; dense or sparse storage; ordering and pivoting; symbolic and numeric factors; and temporary workspace. Under one fixed implementation model, peak memory is the maximum simultaneous storage of model data, factors, and workspace. No universal monotonic relation between block length and peak memory holds without these choices, because fewer macro-stages compete with larger dense blocks and factor fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condensing memory is implementation-relative and includes data, factors, and workspace; larger blocks need not monotonically raise or lower peak memory.
assumptions_latex: All compared partitions use one declared storage and factorization model.
Peak simultaneous scalar storage is the comparison metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{mem}(P)=\max_t\{\operatorname{data}_t(P)+\operatorname{factors}_t(P)+\operatorname{workspace}_t(P)\},\quad\text{with no universal monotonicity in block length}.

notation.meaning: peak memory under the declared implementation model

knowledge_statements.title: Implementation-Relative Peak Memory
Memory-Footprint Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural storage bound for macro-stage data and a banded block factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let block \(j\) contain \(L_j\) controls and define \(w_j=n_x+L_jn_u\). Storing dense quadratic and constraint data local to that macro-stage requires \(O(w_j^2)\) scalars, so all macro-stage data require \(O(\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}w_j^2)\) storage. For a direct factorization that respects the path ordering and has uniformly bounded block bandwidth, factor storage has the same structural order. Hence it is \(O(M(n_x+L_{max}n_u)^2)\); with fixed \(n_x\), \(n_u\), and bounded \(L_{max}\), memory is \(O(M)\), whereas full condensation can require \(O((Nn_u)^2)\) Hessian storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded condensing blocks give memory linear in the number of macro-stages; full condensation may require quadratic storage in the horizon control dimension.
assumptions_latex: Macro-stage matrices are stored as dense blocks.
The factorization follows a path ordering with uniformly bounded block bandwidth.
Only asymptotic scalar storage is counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Storage is \(O(\sum_j(n_x+L_jn_u)^2)\), bounded by \(O(M(n_x+L_{\max}n_u)^2)\).

notation.meaning: number of original stages in block j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits, but the storage estimate additionally requires bounds on local constraint and multiplier dimensions and on factorization fill. The statement also alternates between L_{max} and L_{\max}. An authoritative complexity source is required.

children.title: Condensing Tradeoff Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Structural comparisons among competing dimension, sparsity, and memory outcomes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extraction of nondominated condensing choices from a finite candidate family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(K=|\mathscr P|\) evaluated resource vectors \(r(P)\in\mathbb R^q\), retain \(P\) exactly when no \(P'\) satisfies \(r(P')\le r(P)\) componentwise with at least one strict component. Pairwise dominance testing returns the exact frontier using \(O(qK^2)\) scalar comparisons. A discarded point has a dominating-candidate witness; membership of a retained point is established by exhaustive absence of a dominator in the enumerated family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise dominance filtering extracts a finite condensing frontier and supplies a dominating witness for every rejected point.
assumptions_latex: Every admissible candidate and all declared resource measures have been evaluated.
All measures use the same computational model and are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathscr F=\{P\in\mathscr P:\nexists P'\in\mathscr P,\ r(P')\le r(P),\ r(P')\ne r(P)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Frontier Extraction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of scalarized selection on a discrete condensing-resource frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\) minimizes \(w^{\mathsf T}r(P)\) over \(\mathscr P\) for some \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^q\), then \(P\) is nondominated. The converse can fail for a discrete nonconvex resource image: nondominated points outside the supported lower faces of \(\operatorname{conv}(r(\mathscr P))+\mathbb R_+^q\) are not selected by any strictly positive weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive weighted sums produce nondominated choices but can miss unsupported points of a discrete condensing frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathscr P\) is finite and every resource coordinate is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{Q\in\mathscr P}w^{\mathsf T}r(Q)\Rightarrow P\in\mathscr F,\quad\text{but not conversely in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Sum Coverage Boundary
Condensing Tradeoff Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier over admissible horizon partitions and solver-resource measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathscr P\) be a finite family of admissible condensing partitions. For \(P\in\mathscr P\), let \(d(P)\) be the resulting decision dimension, \(s(P)\) a sparsity-loss measure, and \(m(P)\) a predicted memory requirement, all to be minimized. A partition \(P\) lies on the condensing tradeoff frontier if no \(P'\in\mathscr P\) satisfies
\[d(P')\le d(P),\qquad s(P')\le s(P),\qquad m(P')\le m(P),\]
with at least one strict inequality. The frontier therefore contains precisely the nondominated choices under the declared measures and computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A condensing partition is frontier-optimal when no other admissible partition weakly improves dimension, sparsity loss, and memory while strictly improving one.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathscr P\) is a finite nonempty set of admissible partitions.
The measures \(d\), \(s\), and \(m\) use one fixed solver and storage model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tradeoff frontier is the set of nondominated partitions in \((d,s,m)\)-space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nondominance definition correctly matches the frontier leaf, but the candidate supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Fixed Blocking Structures
children.top_down_role: Move-blocked MPC parameterizations using a predetermined repeated block pattern.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical family showing strict suboptimality when the prescribed blocks exclude the unblocked optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(\bar U\notin\operatorname{range}(T)\), consider the unconstrained strongly convex QP \(\min_U\tfrac12\|U-\bar U\|_2^2\). Its unblocked optimizer is \(\bar U\) with value zero, whereas its fixed-blocked value is \(\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}(\bar U,\operatorname{range}(T))^2>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic centered at a sequence that violates the fixed blocks gives a strict and quantitatively characterized blocking loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_B-p=\tfrac12\operatorname{dist}(\bar U,\operatorname{range}(T))^2>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Loss Family for Fixed Blocking

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Restriction, and Exactness of Fixed Blocking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of a fixed full-column-rank move-blocking lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb R^{Nn_u\times Bn_u}\) be the incidence lifting of a nonempty fixed partition. Then \(T\) has full column rank. If \(H\succeq0\), then \(T^{\mathsf T}HT\succeq0\); if \(H\succ0\), then \(T^{\mathsf T}HT\succ0\). For original feasible set \(\mathcal F\), fixed blocking restricts feasible inputs to \(\mathcal F_B=\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{range}(T)\), so the blocked minimization value satisfies \(p_B\ge p\). Provided the original optimum is attained, \(p_B=p\) exactly when an original optimizer belongs to \(\operatorname{range}(T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed blocking preserves convexity, inherits positive definiteness, restricts feasibility, and is lossless exactly when an original optimizer obeys the prescribed blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is generated by a nonempty fixed consecutive partition.
The original problem has an attained finite optimum.
The blocked problem is feasible when its finite optimal value is discussed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T^{\mathsf T}HT\succeq0,\qquad p_B\ge p,\qquad p_B=p\iff\operatorname*{argmin}_{U\in\mathcal F}f(U)\cap\operatorname{range}(T)\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: feasible input sequences satisfying the fixed pattern

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity, Restriction, and Exactness of Fixed Blocking
Fixed Blocking Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Move-blocking by a fixed consecutive partition of the control horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix boundaries \(0=c_0<c_1<\cdots<c_B=N\) before solving and introduce block moves \(v_0,\ldots,v_{B-1}\). The fixed blocking constraint is
\[u_k=v_j\quad\text{for}\quad c_j\le k<c_{j+1},\]
or, after stacking, \(U=Tv\), where \(T\) is the block-indicator lifting matrix. Substituting into a control QP with Hessian \(H\), gradient \(g\), and constraints \(\ell\le CU\le u\) gives
\[\min_v\ \tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}T^{\mathsf T}HTv+(T^{\mathsf T}g)^{\mathsf T}v\quad\text{subject to}\quad \ell\le CTv\le u.\]
The feasible input sequences are exactly those constant on every prescribed block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed move-blocking pattern replaces all controls in each prescribed interval by one shared decision and transforms the QP through a lifting matrix.
assumptions_latex: The blocking boundaries are fixed independently of the optimization variables.
Each stage belongs to exactly one consecutive blocking interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed blocking restricts controls to \(U=Tv\) and produces the reduced Hessian \(T^{\mathsf T}HT\).

notation.meaning: shared control move for block j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed move-blocking representation and reduced QP are coherent, but no inspectable MPC move-blocking source is cited.

children.title: Variable Blocking Structures
children.top_down_role: Move-blocked MPC parameterizations using nonuniform or adaptable block lengths.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonconvex Union from Endogenous Block Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal family showing why endogenous selection is not generally one continuous QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scalar inputs over three stages, consider the two two-block patterns \(S_1=\{U:u_0=u_1\}\) and \(S_2=\{U:u_1=u_2\}\). If the optimizer may choose either pattern, its admissible set is \(S_1\cup S_2\), which is nonconvex: \((0,0,1)\in S_1\) and \((1,0,0)\in S_2\), but their midpoint belongs to neither set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing between two blocking patterns can create a nonconvex union of linear subspaces.
assumptions_latex: The blocking pattern is an endogenous discrete choice.
Inputs are scalar over three stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_1\cup S_2\text{ is nonconvex}.

notation.meaning: input subspaces induced by two alternative patterns

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Union from Endogenous Block Selection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exogenous solve-wise pattern selection from optimization over the pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each fixed parameter value \(\theta\), substituting \(U=(B(\theta)\otimes I_{n_u})V\) into a convex horizon QP produces a continuous convex QP. If the block assignment or block count is instead an optimization decision, the admissible input set is generally a union of pattern-specific linear images; encoding that choice generally requires a mixed-integer or disjunctive model rather than one continuous QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable pattern yields a convex QP after exogenous selection; optimizing the pattern generally leaves the continuous-QP class.
assumptions_latex: \(B(\theta)\) is fixed throughout each QP solve.
The underlying horizon objective is convex quadratic and its constraints are affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(\theta)\text{ fixed}\Longrightarrow\text{continuous convex QP};\qquad B\text{ optimized}\Longrightarrow\text{generally a disjunctive or mixed-integer model}.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-QP Boundary for Variable Blocking
Variable Blocking Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Online-selectable, solve-wise fixed input blocking for a finite MPC horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a prediction horizon of length \(N\), a variable blocking structure is a parameter-indexed family of matrices \(B(\theta)\in\{0,1\}^{N\times M(\theta)}\) whose rows each contain exactly one nonzero entry and whose equal-column row sets are consecutive intervals. The predicted input sequence is restricted by \[U=(B(\theta)\otimes I_{n_u})V.\] The block boundaries and the number \(M(\theta)\leq N\) may vary with the measured parameter \(\theta\), but \(B(\theta)\) is fixed before the associated QP is solved. Thus every component of \(V\) specifies one constant input move over its assigned interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable blocking selects consecutive input blocks from the measured parameter, fixes them before optimization, and assigns one decision vector to each block.
assumptions_latex: \(B(\theta)\) is fixed during each QP solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=(B(\theta)\otimes I_{n_u})V\) defines a linear move-blocking restriction for each fixed \(\theta\).

children.title: Blocking-Granularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes distinguished by coarse, fine, or horizon-varying move resolution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility and optimal-value ordering across nested blocking granularities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let partition \(\mathcal P_f\) refine \(\mathcal P_c\), with representable input subspaces \(\mathcal U_c\subseteq\mathcal U_f\). For the same objective \(f\) and unblocked feasible set \(\mathcal F\), \[\mathcal F\cap\mathcal U_c\subseteq\mathcal F\cap\mathcal U_f.\] Thus coarse feasibility implies fine feasibility, and when both problems have finite attained minima, \(v_f\le v_c\). At the stagewise partition \(M=N\), the blocked problem is the unblocked problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refining a block partition cannot remove feasible inputs or worsen a finite attained minimum; the finest partition recovers the unblocked QP.
assumptions_latex: The finer fixed partition subdivides every block of the coarse partition.
Both formulations use the same objective and original constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_c\subseteq\mathcal F_f\) and \(v_f\le v_c\), with exact unblocked recovery at \(M=N\).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Partition Refinement
Blocking-Granularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by the number of independent moves retained over the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be the input horizon and let \(B\in\{0,1\}^{N\times M}\) encode \(M\) nonempty consecutive blocks. The granularity regimes are: full blocking when \(M=1\), so all predicted inputs coincide; intermediate blocking when \(1<M<N\); and unblocked control when \(M=N\) and \(B=I_N\). For \(n_u\) input components, the number of input decision variables is \(Mn_u\), compared with \(Nn_u\) in the unblocked formulation. Refining a partition only enlarges its representable input subspace, while coarsening it only restricts that subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Blocking ranges from one horizon-wide move through intermediate partitions to one move per stage; finer partitions retain more input freedom and variables.
assumptions_latex: Every block is nonempty and consists of consecutive stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained input dimension is \(Mn_u\), and refinement produces a nested enlargement of the admissible input subspace.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary dimension and subspace consequences of linear move blocking
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classification and nested-subspace claim are mathematically plausible and fit the container, but the record provides no citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Move-Blocking Structures
children.top_down_role: MPC horizon reductions obtained by sharing input decisions across stages.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of inputs representable by a fixed consecutive blocking matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_b=B\otimes I_{n_u}\) encode nonempty disjoint blocks of lengths \(L_1,\ldots,L_M\). Then \[T_b^{\mathsf T}T_b=\operatorname{diag}(L_1,\ldots,L_M)\otimes I_{n_u},\qquad P_b=T_b(T_b^{\mathsf T}T_b)^{-1}T_b^{\mathsf T}.\] The matrix \(P_b\) is the orthogonal projector onto the blocked-input subspace, and \(U\) is representable exactly when \(P_bU=U\), equivalently when the inputs are constant within every block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The blocking matrix's orthogonal projector gives an exact test for whether a full input sequence obeys the prescribed block pattern.
assumptions_latex: The blocks are nonempty, disjoint, consecutive, and cover the horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U\in\operatorname{range}(T_b)\iff P_bU=U.

Move-Blocking Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix representation of consecutive, fixed input moves in an MPC QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose boundaries \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_M=N\) and define \(B\in\{0,1\}^{N\times M}\) by \(B_{kj}=1\) exactly when \(t_{j-1}\leq k<t_j\). If \(v_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n_u}\) is the move assigned to block \(j\), then the stacked horizon input satisfies \[U=T_bV,\qquad T_b=B\otimes I_{n_u},\qquad V=(v_1^\top,\ldots,v_M^\top)^\top.\] Because the blocks are nonempty, \(T_b\) has full column rank. Substitution of this relation into any QP objective or affine constraint preserves quadraticity and affinity, respectively.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=T_bV\) is an injective linear representation of the move-blocked input subspace.

children.title: Condensing Structures
children.top_down_role: MPC horizon reductions obtained by eliminating state or intermediate variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination of states within horizon segments while retaining selected boundary states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose checkpoints \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_p=N\). Within each segment, repeated dynamics substitution expresses every interior state affinely in \(x_{\tau_i}\) and the segment inputs. Eliminating only interior states yields an exact QP in checkpoint states and inputs, coupled between adjacent segments by checkpoint-transition equations. Full condensing is obtained when no predicted checkpoint state is retained; the sparse form is obtained when every predicted stage state is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial condensing eliminates states inside horizon segments while retaining checkpoint states, interpolating exactly between sparse and fully condensed formulations.
assumptions_latex: The horizon dynamics are explicit and affine.
All eliminated interior states are substituted exactly throughout the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partial condensing preserves feasible trajectories and objective values while exposing segment-level coupling.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Condensing by State Checkpoints
Condensing Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination of predicted states from linear-dynamics MPC QPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dynamics \(x_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k+d_k\), stacking \(X=(x_1^\top,\ldots,x_N^\top)^\top\) and \(U=(u_0^\top,\ldots,u_{N-1}^\top)^\top\) gives \[X=S_xx_0+S_uU+s.\] Substituting this affine identity into a convex quadratic stage-cost model produces a condensed objective \(\tfrac12U^\top H_cU+h_c(x_0)^\top U+c(x_0)\), with \(H_c\succeq0\), and converts affine state-input constraints into affine constraints on \(U\). Since the forward dynamics determine \(X\) uniquely from \((x_0,U)\), the sparse and fully condensed formulations have identical feasible inputs and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condensing uses forward dynamics to eliminate all predicted states, yielding an equivalent convex QP in the stacked inputs alone.
assumptions_latex: The horizon dynamics are affine and explicit in \(x_{k+1}\).
The original cost has a positive-semidefinite quadratic Hessian.
All modeled constraints are affine in states and inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution \(X=S_xx_0+S_uU+s\) yields an equivalent condensed convex QP in \(U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Blocking-Condensing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint state elimination and fixed linear input blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the condensed dynamics be \(X=S_xx_0+S_uU+s\), and impose the fixed move-blocking relation \(U=T_bV\). Their joint substitution is \[X=S_xx_0+S_uT_bV+s,\qquad U=T_bV.\] If the unblocked condensed objective is \(\tfrac12U^\top H_cU+h_c(x_0)^\top U+c(x_0)\), the blocked-condensed Hessian is \(H_{bc}=T_b^\top H_cT_b\succeq0\). Affine constraints remain affine in \(V\). The resulting QP is equivalent to the original sparse MPC problem restricted to input sequences in \(\operatorname{range}(T_b)\), independently of whether blocking or exact state elimination is substituted first.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combining exact state elimination with fixed move blocking gives a convex QP in block moves and restricts the original problem to the blocking subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_{bc}=T_b^\top H_cT_b\succeq0\), and the feasible input set equals the original feasible set intersected with \(\operatorname{range}(T_b)\).

children.title: Reduction-Interaction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where combined reductions impair sparsity, flexibility, or numerical balance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal failure example for restriction to a blocked-input subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two scalar inputs subject to \(u_0=0\) and \(u_1=1\), with zero objective. The unblocked QP is feasible. One-block move blocking imposes \(u_0=u_1=v\), which is incompatible with both requirements, so the blocked QP is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharing one move across two stages can make a previously feasible affine problem infeasible.
assumptions_latex: A single block covers both input stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\) does not imply \(\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{range}(T_b)\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditioning Is Not Preserved by Blocking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical scaling boundary of the blocked-condensed congruence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when \(H_c=I\), consecutive blocking with positive block lengths \(L_1,\ldots,L_M\) gives \[T_b^{\mathsf T}H_cT_b=\operatorname{diag}(L_1,\ldots,L_M)\otimes I_{n_u}.\] Therefore its spectral condition number is \(\max_jL_j/\min_jL_j\), although \(\kappa_2(H_c)=1\). Column normalization of \(T_b\) removes this particular scaling imbalance without changing its range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal block lengths can worsen Hessian conditioning even when the original condensed Hessian is perfectly conditioned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(T_b^{\mathsf T}H_cT_b)\) can exceed \(\kappa_2(H_c)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Is Not Preserved by Blocking

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restriction Can Lose Feasibility or Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-set and optimal-value losses caused by fixed move blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an original feasible input set \(\mathcal F\) and fixed blocking map \(T_b\), the blocked feasible set is \(\mathcal F_b=\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{range}(T_b)\). Hence \(\mathcal F_b\) may be empty even when \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\). If both minimization problems attain finite optima, then \(v_b\ge v\), with strict inequality possible unless an original optimizer lies in \(\operatorname{range}(T_b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move blocking restricts the feasible inputs, so it can destroy feasibility or produce a strictly worse optimum.
assumptions_latex: The blocking map is fixed and linear.
The blocked and unblocked problems otherwise use the same objective and constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_b\subseteq\mathcal F\) and, when finite attained optima exist, \(v_b\ge v\).
knowledge_statements.title: Restriction Can Lose Feasibility or Optimality
Reduction-Interaction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which blocking and condensing cease to be exact commuting linear reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Blocking and condensing commute as QP-preserving substitutions when \(U=T_bV\) is fixed and linear and the dynamics uniquely give \(X=S_xx_0+S_uU+s\). This boundary is crossed if either substitution is not a fixed affine map. For example, if a block assignment is selected by a component of \(V\), then \(T_b=T_b(V)\) makes \(U=T_b(V)V\) generally nonlinear or disjunctive, so the reduced model is not a single convex QP. Likewise, descriptor dynamics \(E_kx_{k+1}=A_kx_k+B_ku_k\) with singular \(E_k\) do not admit the stated full-condensing map unless additional solvability and uniqueness conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reductions commute only as fixed affine substitutions; decision-dependent blocks or non-uniquely solvable dynamics can destroy the single convex-QP representation.
assumptions_latex: The intended reduced model is a single continuous convex QP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decision-dependent blocking or failure of unique affine state elimination invalidates the standard commuting reduction formula.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condensed multiparametric QP with the measured state as parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state-parameterized finite-horizon linear MPC problem can be written as \[V(x)=\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{n_z}}\left\{\tfrac12z^\top Hz+(Fx+f)^\top z+\tfrac12x^\top Yx+y^\top x+c: Gz\leq W+Sx\right\},\] where the measured state \(x\in\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_x}\) is a parameter and \(H\succeq0\). This form results from stacking or condensing linear prediction dynamics and affine constraints. If \(H\succ0\) and the feasible set is nonempty, the optimizer \(z^*(x)\) is unique; the applied MPC input is an affine projection \(u(x)=K_zz^*(x)+K_xx+k\).

children.title: Critical-Region Geometry
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral organization of parameter-space regions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the regular affine critical-region construction when the fixed-active-set KKT matrix is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate active set \(I\), write \[M_I\begin{bmatrix}z\\lambda_I\end{bmatrix}=b_I(x),\qquad M_I=\begin{bmatrix}H&G_I^\top\\G_I&0\end{bmatrix}.\] If \(M_I\) is nonsingular, the primal-dual solution is a unique affine function of \(x\), and its validity set is polyhedral. If \(M_I\) is singular, the system may be inconsistent or have multiple primal-dual solutions; the regular unique-affine construction cannot then be inferred without degeneracy resolution or elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard affine critical-region construction requires a nonsingular active-set KKT matrix; singularity can cause inconsistency or nonunique primal-dual solutions.
assumptions_latex: The QP data depend affinely on the parameter.
\(I\) is a fixed candidate active set.

Critical-Region Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral parameter regions induced by a fixed nondegenerate optimal active set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the state-parameterized QP with \(H\succ0\). Fix an index set \(I\) whose active constraint gradients are linearly independent. Solving the equality-constrained KKT system for \(I\) gives affine functions \(z_I(x)=K_Ix+k_I\) and \(\lambda_I(x)=L_Ix+\ell_I\). Its critical region is \[\mathcal R_I=\{x\in\mathcal X:G_Iz_I(x)=W_I+S_Ix,\ G_{\bar I}z_I(x)\leq W_{\bar I}+S_{\bar I}x,\ \lambda_I(x)\geq0\}.\] Hence \(\mathcal R_I\) is a possibly empty closed polyhedron; its relative interior is obtained by making nonredundant inactive-slack and positive-multiplier inequalities strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed regular active set, affine KKT solutions turn primal and dual feasibility into linear inequalities, so its critical region is polyhedral.
assumptions_latex: The rows of \(G_I\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_I\) is a possibly empty polyhedron in parameter space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension of an Exact Active Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension and relative openness of the primal locus associated with one exact activity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\) and let \(P(x)=\{z:Gz\le W+Sx\}\). If \[F_I^\circ(x)=\{z:G_Iz=W_I+S_Ix,\ G_{\bar I}z<W_{\bar I}+S_{\bar I}x\}\] is nonempty, it is relatively open in \(\{z:G_Iz=W_I+S_Ix\}\), its closure is obtained by replacing the strict inequalities by weak inequalities, and \[\dim F_I^\circ(x)=n-\operatorname{rank}(G_I).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty exact active-set locus is the relative interior of a polyhedral face and has dimension equal to the decision dimension minus the rank of its active normals.
assumptions_latex: \(P(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is described by affine inequalities.
The exact activity locus \(F_I^\circ(x)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim F_I^\circ(x)=n-\operatorname{rank}(G_I).

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension of an Exact Active Face
Active-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual parameter locus associated with a prescribed constraint activity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parametric feasible polyhedron \(P(x)=\{z:Gz\leq W+Sx\}\), define the active set at \((z,x)\) by \(\mathcal A(z,x)=\{i:G_iz=W_i+S_ix\}\). For a prescribed set \(I\), the primal locus having exactly that activity pattern is \[\mathcal F_I=\{(z,x):G_Iz=W_I+S_Ix,\ G_{\bar I}z<W_{\bar I}+S_{\bar I}x\}.\] Its closure replaces the strict inequalities by weak inequalities and is polyhedral. Optimal active-set geometry additionally intersects this locus with stationarity \(Hz+Fx+f+G_I^\top\lambda_I=0\) and dual feasibility \(\lambda_I\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An activity pattern defines a relatively open polyhedral face locus; imposing stationarity and nonnegative multipliers selects the portion that can be optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed active set determines a polyhedral primal face locus and, after KKT conditions are imposed, an optimality locus.

children.title: Region-to-Active-Set Correspondence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant-constraint example distinguishing the exact tight set from nonunique multiplier-support or KKT-basis labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min_z\ \tfrac12(z-\theta)^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad z\le0,\quad 2z\le0.\] For every \(\theta>0\), the unique optimizer is \(z^*(\theta)=0\), and the exact tight set is \(\{1,2\}\). Stationarity, \(-\theta+\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0\), admits nonnegative multipliers supported on \(\{1\}\), \(\{2\}\), or \(\{1,2\}\). Hence one full-dimensional parameter region has one exact tight set but several valid multiplier-support or KKT-basis labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant active constraints preserve the exact tight set but can give one critical region several valid multiplier-support or working-set labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\theta>0\}\text{ has one exact tight set but multiple valid KKT support labels}.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Destroys Unique Working-Set Labels
Region-to-Active-Set Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate correspondence between full-dimensional critical regions and optimal active sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strictly convex parametric QP, suppose that throughout the relative interior of a full-dimensional critical region the optimal active gradients are linearly independent and strict complementarity holds. Then the optimizer and active multipliers are affine there, and the same optimal active set \(I\) occurs at every interior parameter. Conversely, any active set satisfying these regularity conditions and having a nonempty full-dimensional primal-dual feasibility region defines one critical region after redundant inequalities are removed. On shared region boundaries, zero inactive slacks or zero active multipliers can make several active-set descriptions valid, so one-to-one correspondence is asserted only for region interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under LICQ and strict complementarity, each full-dimensional region interior has one optimal active set; boundary points may admit multiple active-set descriptions.
assumptions_latex: LICQ and strict complementarity hold on each considered region interior.
The considered critical regions are full-dimensional relative to \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full-dimensional critical-region interiors correspond one-to-one with regular optimal active sets, while boundary correspondence may be nonunique.

For a finite closed cover, this agreement also makes the resulting map continuous.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonunique Optimizers Do Not Necessarily Define a Unique Explicit Law
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimizer-to-controller boundary when strict convexity or a selection rule is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a feasible parametric convex QP has multiple optimizers at a parameter \(x\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}_z Q(z,x)\) is set-valued. Its projection onto the applied input does not define a unique control value unless every optimizer has the same projected first input or a deterministic selection rule is specified. Thus positive-semidefinite curvature alone does not imply a unique continuous piecewise-affine control law.

children.title: Explicit-MPC Storage Layouts
children.top_down_role: Representations for stored regions, gains, offsets, plus adjacency metadata.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compressed storage when critical regions reuse facet hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every region inequality is selected, with an orientation, from \(M\) stored affine hyperplanes \((a_j,b_j)\). Store this dictionary and, for each region \(i\), an incidence list \(L_i\), orientation signs \(\sigma_{ij}\), and its affine law \((F_i,g_i)\). Then \[\mathcal R_i=\bigcap_{j\in L_i}\{x:\sigma_{ij}(a_j^\top x-b_j)\le0\}.\] Lossless incidence data therefore represent the same controller as duplicated per-region arrays. Dense coefficient storage is \(M(p+1)+Rr(p+1)\) real scalars, plus incidence metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated region facets can be stored once in a hyperplane dictionary, with each region holding lossless incidence references and its affine law.
assumptions_latex: Every region inequality is represented exactly by a dictionary entry and orientation.
There are \(R\) regions, parameter dimension \(p\), and output dimension \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_i=\bigcap_{j\in L_i}\{x:\sigma_{ij}(a_j^\top x-b_j)\le0\},\quad\text{with the represented map unchanged}.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Hyperplane Dictionary Layout
Explicit-MPC Storage Layouts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite data representations supporting exact region lookup and affine-law evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicit law \(u(x)=F_ix+g_i\) on regions \(\mathcal R_i=\{x:H_ix\leq h_i\}\), an exact flat layout stores the tuples \((H_i,h_i,F_i,g_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,R\). A linked layout additionally stores region adjacency, while a search layout stores internal predicates \(a_j^\top x\leq b_j\) and leaf-to-region indices in a decision tree or directed acyclic graph. A valid layout must return an index \(i\) satisfying \(H_ix\leq h_i\) for every \(x\) in the covered domain and then output \(F_ix+g_i\). Boundary tie-breaking may select any incident region whose affine laws agree at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit MPC stores region inequalities and affine gains, optionally with adjacency or search indices; lookup must return a containing region before evaluating its law.
assumptions_latex: The explicit law has finitely many polyhedral regions.
Affine laws agree wherever stored closed regions overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each valid layout represents the same mapping \(x\mapsto u(x)\) when its point-location procedure returns a containing region.

children.title: Critical-Region Point-Location Interfaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical boundary for half-space point location in an explicit controller.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_i=\{\theta:H_i\theta\le h_i\}\). Suppose each entry of \(\Delta H_i\) is bounded by \(\varepsilon_H\), each entry of \(\Delta h_i\) by \(\varepsilon_h\), and \(\|\Delta\theta\|_\infty\le\varepsilon_\theta\). For row \(j\), \[|((H_i+\Delta H_i)(\theta+\Delta\theta)-(h_i+\Delta h_i))_j-(H_i\theta-h_i)_j|\le \varepsilon_H\|\theta\|_1+(\|H_{i,j}\|_1+p\varepsilon_H)\varepsilon_\theta+\varepsilon_h.\] A residual sign is certified only when its distance from zero exceeds this bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half-space membership is sign-certain only when residuals are separated from zero by more than the data and query error bound; facet-near queries require explicit tie and fallback policies.
assumptions_latex: The perturbation bounds are componentwise uniform.
Membership is decided from half-space residual signs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\widehat r_{ij}-r_{ij}|\le\varepsilon_H\|\theta\|_1+(\|H_{i,j}\|_1+p\varepsilon_H)\varepsilon_\theta+\varepsilon_h.

notation.meaning: Bounds on stored-data and query perturbations.

Each stored affine law is valid throughout its associated region.
For every overlap \(\mathcal R_i\cap\mathcal R_j\), the stored laws agree: \(K_i\theta+k_i=K_j\theta+k_j\) for all \(\theta\in\mathcal R_i\cap\mathcal R_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta\in\mathcal R_i\Longrightarrow u(\theta)=K_i\theta+k_i\).

affine control law on region i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact online lookup for a stored polyhedral explicit-MPC partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Store regions \(\mathcal R_i=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^p:H_i\theta\le h_i\}\) and associated affine laws \(u_i(\theta)=K_i\theta+k_i\), for \(i=1,\ldots,N\). Given \(\theta\), a point-location interface returns an index \(i\) satisfying \(H_i\theta\le h_i\) and then outputs \(u_i(\theta)\). If several closed regions contain a boundary point, use a fixed deterministic tie rule. When the stored laws agree on region overlaps, the selected control is independent of that rule. If no region contains \(\theta\), return an out-of-domain status rather than extrapolating a law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locate the parameter in a stored critical region, evaluate its affine control law, resolve boundary ties deterministically, and report parameters outside the partition; tie independence requires the laws to agree on overlaps.

children.title: Storage–Lookup Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Memory, latency, plus indexing tradeoffs in explicit controllers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic latency boundary for deterministic binary indexed lookup among stored regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic binary decision tree of worst-case depth \(d\) has at most \(2^d\) leaves. If its leaves distinguish \(N\) region labels, then \[d\ge\lceil\log_2N\rceil.\] A full binary tree with \(N\) leaves has exactly \(N-1\) internal predicate nodes. Thus binary indexing cannot have sublogarithmic worst-case predicate depth, and its explicit tree representation requires linearly many leaf and internal-node records. Geometric restrictions may force greater depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary lookup tree for N regions needs at least logarithmic worst-case depth and linear node storage; geometry can require deeper trees.
assumptions_latex: Each terminal outcome identifies one of \(N\) distinguishable region labels.
Every internal node has two outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\ge\lceil\log_2N\rceil,\qquad n_{\mathrm{internal}}=N-1\ \text{for a full binary tree with }N\text{ leaves}.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Lookup Depth–Storage Bound

assumptions_latex: The controller is represented by finitely many polyhedral regions and affine laws.
Each \(H_i\) is stored densely, each control law has output dimension \(r\), and costs count stored scalars and scalar inequality tests up to constant factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A direct representation stores \(\Theta\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N(q_i+r)(p+1)\right)\) scalars, while a linear scan may test \(\sum_{i=1}^N q_i\) inequalities in the worst case; an auxiliary index can exchange additional storage for fewer online region tests.

notation.meaning: number of inequalities describing region i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct storage accounting follows from the dimensions of the halfspace and affine-law arrays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory and online comparison costs for explicit-MPC region representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear scan of \(N\) regions \(\mathcal R_i=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^p:H_i\theta\le h_i\}\), let \(H_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i\times p}\), \(h_i\in\mathbb R^{q_i}\), and let the associated law be \(u_i(\theta)=K_i\theta+k_i\in\mathbb R^r\). Dense storage of all halfspaces and affine laws uses \(\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(q_i(p+1)+r(p+1)\bigr)\) scalars, while a linear scan may test \(\sum_{i=1}^N q_i\) scalar inequalities in the worst case. An auxiliary search tree or spatial index may reduce online region tests at the cost of additional nodes and partition data. The resulting storage and lookup costs depend on the representation, partition, and query distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense direct storage scales with all halfspace coefficients and affine-law coefficients. A linear scan can require testing every stored inequality, while an auxiliary search structure can reduce lookup work by using additional memory.
knowledge_statements.title: Storage–Lookup Tradeoffs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strictly convex separable mpQP family exhibiting exponential full-dimensional region growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge1\), consider \[\min_{z\in\mathbb R^d}\tfrac12\|z-\theta\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad0\le z_i\le1.\] Its optimizer is \(z_i^*(\theta)=\min\{1,\max\{0,\theta_i\}\}\). Each coordinate has the three open regimes \(\theta_i<0\), \(0<\theta_i<1\), and \(\theta_i>1\). Their Cartesian products give exactly \(3^d\) full-dimensional critical regions. With \(m=2d\) inequalities, \(N=3^{m/2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a d-dimensional box has three regimes per coordinate and therefore 3^d full-dimensional critical regions, proving exponential growth.
assumptions_latex: The parameter domain intersects every Cartesian product of the three coordinate regimes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N=3^d=3^{m/2},\qquad m=2d.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Critical-Region Family

assumptions_latex: The parametric QP is strictly convex in its decision variable and has \(m\) scalar inequalities.
Every full-dimensional critical region is assigned a unique optimal active set.
For each active set, its parameter-validity set contributes at most one full-dimensional critical region.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: under the stated injection, critical regions are counted by subsets of the inequality index set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-set counting boundary for nondegenerate multiparametric convex QPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a strictly convex multiparametric QP with \(m\) scalar inequalities. If every full-dimensional critical region is assigned a unique optimal active set and each active set contributes at most one full-dimensional parameter-validity region, then the assignment injects the full-dimensional critical regions into the \(2^m\) subsets of the inequality index set. Consequently, the number \(N\) of full-dimensional critical regions satisfies \(N\le 2^m\). Degenerate active-set descriptions must be identified or assigned consistently before applying this count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated uniqueness and single-validity-region assumptions, full-dimensional critical regions inject into the active-set subsets, so there are at most two to the power m such regions.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-MPC Region-Complexity Boundary
