children.title: Active-Set Instability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of the identified active set to perturbations, scaling, or tolerances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active-Set Switching at a Weakly Active Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional parametric QP demonstrating failure of local active-set constancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t\in\mathbb R\), consider
\[\min_{x\ge0}\ \tfrac12x^2-tx.\]
For the inequality \(-x\le0\), the unique primal solution and its multiplier are
\[(x(t),z(t))=\begin{cases}(t,0),&t>0,\\(0,0),&t=0,\\(0,-t),&t<0.\end{cases}\]
Thus the constraint is inactive for \(t>0\), weakly active at \(t=0\), and strongly active for \(t<0\). Arbitrarily small perturbations around zero therefore change the active set despite strict convexity and a unique primal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar strictly convex QP switches between inactive and strongly active regimes under arbitrarily small perturbations around a weakly active solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active set is not locally constant at \(t=0\).
review_flags: Elementary parametric QP; all solution and multiplier values are explicitly checkable.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Switching at a Weakly Active Solution
Active-Set Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional parametric QP exhibiting active-set switching at a weakly active solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t\in\mathbb R\), consider
\[\min_{x\ge0}\ \tfrac12x^2-tx.\]
Its unique solution and multiplier for the inequality \(-x\le0\) are
\[(x(t),z(t))=\begin{cases}(t,0),&t>0,\\(0,0),&t=0,\\(0,-t),&t<0.\end{cases}\]
At \(t=0\), the inequality is weakly active. Every positive perturbation makes it inactive, whereas every negative perturbation makes it strongly active. Hence arbitrarily small data perturbations change the active set at the weak-activity boundary, despite uniqueness and strict convexity of the primal objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar strictly convex QP switches between inactive and strongly active regimes under arbitrarily small perturbations around a weakly active constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active set is not locally constant at \(t=0\).

notation.meaning: multiplier of the inequality minus x less than or equal to zero

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit elementary parametric QP verifies the active-set switching mechanism
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar QP and its piecewise solution correctly exhibit active-status switching, and counterexample is the appropriate kind, but the record supplies no citation.

children.title: Weak-Activity Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundary cases where marginal activity triggers changes in active-set membership.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Activity Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT trichotomy describing transitions through a weakly active inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a KKT solution depending on a parameter \(t\), define the slack \(s_i(t)=-g_i(x(t))\ge0\) and multiplier \(z_i(t)\ge0\). Complementarity gives \(s_i(t)z_i(t)=0\). The local status of inequality \(i\) therefore lies in the trichotomy
\[\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{inactive}&s_i(t)>0&z_i(t)=0\\
\text{weakly active}&s_i(t)=0&z_i(t)=0\\
\text{strongly active}&s_i(t)=0&z_i(t)>0.
\end{array}\]
A weak-activity transition is a parameter value at which a solution path passes through the middle regime while adjoining parameter values occupy at least one of the other regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity yields inactive, weakly active, and strongly active regimes; a weak-activity transition passes through zero slack and zero multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak activity is the boundary regime \(s_i(t)=z_i(t)=0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complementarity trichotomy is internally consistent and representation is a suitable kind for this regime table, but no inspectable source supports the terminology.

children.title: Nearly Singular Curvature Matrices
children.top_down_role: Curvature degeneracy arising from flat, weakly penalized, or correlated variable directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient Weak Curvature May Be Inactive
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between ambient Hessian conditioning and effective conditioning on feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(\varepsilon,1)\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and impose \(x_1=0\). The ambient condition number is \(\kappa_2(Q)=\varepsilon^{-1}\), but the feasible direction space is \(\operatorname{span}\{(0,1)\}\), on which the reduced Hessian is \([1]\). Thus ambient near-singularity need not imply weak effective curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraints can exclude a weak eigenvector, leaving the reduced curvature perfectly conditioned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(Q)=\varepsilon^{-1}\) while \(\kappa_2(Z^{\mathsf T}QZ)=1\).

notation.meaning: basis for the feasible direction space

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Weak Curvature May Be Inactive

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance of Positive-Definite Curvature to Singularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise perturbation characterization of near-singular symmetric curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), then \[\min\{\|E\|_2:Q+E\text{ is singular},\ E=E^{\mathsf T}\}=\lambda_{\min}(Q).\] Consequently, \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)/\|Q\|_2\) is its relative spectral-norm distance to singularity within symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive-definite curvature, the smallest eigenvalue is exactly the spectral-norm distance to a singular symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_2(Q,\{\text{singular symmetric matrices}\})=\lambda_{\min}(Q).\)

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of the curvature matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Distance of Positive-Definite Curvature to Singularity
Nearly Singular Curvature Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral threshold condition for positive-semidefinite QP curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q=Q^\top\succeq0\) be nonzero and fix a relative tolerance \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). The curvature matrix is \(\varepsilon\)-nearly singular when
\[0<\lambda_{\min}(Q)\le\varepsilon\lVert Q\rVert_2.\]
Equivalently, when \(Q\) is positive definite, its spectral condition number satisfies \(\kappa_2(Q)\ge\varepsilon^{-1}\). If \(\lambda_{\min}(Q)=0\), the matrix is exactly singular rather than merely nearly singular. For constrained QPs, the analogous effective-curvature test may be applied to the reduced Hessian on feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite curvature matrix is nearly singular when its smallest positive spectral scale is tiny relative to its largest spectral scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\lambda_{\min}(Q)\le\varepsilon\lVert Q\rVert_2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relative smallest-singular-value characterization of near singularity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tolerance-dependent spectral condition is coherent and correctly separates exact singularity, but near-singularity is convention-dependent and requires a cited numerical-linear-algebra source.

children.title: Nearly Singular KKT Systems
children.top_down_role: Ill-conditioned saddle-point systems associated with degeneracy or deficient constraint rank.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual certificate for near singularity of a KKT coefficient matrix under fixed scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonzero vector \(z\) and matrix \(K\), \[\sigma_{\min}(K)\le\frac{\|Kz\|_2}{\|z\|_2}.\] Hence, under fixed scaling, \[\|Kz\|_2\le\varepsilon\|K\|_2\|z\|_2\] certifies \(\sigma_{\min}(K)\le\varepsilon\|K\|_2\). If \(Kz=0\), it certifies exact singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector with a small normalized KKT residual certifies a small singular value.
assumptions_latex: The scaling used for \(K\), \(z\), and the residual is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Null-Vector Certificate
Nearly Singular KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative smallest-singular-value criterion for an active-set KKT coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonzero active-set KKT matrix
\[K=\begin{bmatrix}Q&J^\top\\J&0\end{bmatrix}\]
and a tolerance \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), the KKT system is \(\varepsilon\)-nearly singular when
\[0<\sigma_{\min}(K)\le\varepsilon\lVert K\rVert_2.\]
When \(K\) is nonsingular, this is equivalent to \(\kappa_2(K)\ge\varepsilon^{-1}\). Exact equality \(\sigma_{\min}(K)=0\) denotes singularity. The condition is representation-dependent: row, column, and variable scaling can materially change the measured condition number without changing the exact QP solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KKT matrix is nearly singular when its smallest singular value is small relative to its spectral norm, under a specified scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\sigma_{\min}(K)\le\varepsilon\lVert K\rVert_2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relative singular-value condition for near singularity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-value criterion and condition-number equivalence are mathematically consistent, but the threshold convention and scaling qualification require an inspectable source.

children.title: Curvature-Induced KKT Ill-Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Propagation of weak curvature into the conditioning of the full optimality system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coupling between tangent-space curvature and an equality or fixed-active-set KKT matrix when constraint rank is regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker J\), and define \[K=\begin{bmatrix}Q&J^{\mathsf T}\\J&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad H_r=Z^{\mathsf T}QZ,\] where \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\). Then \[K\text{ is nonsingular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H_r\text{ is nonsingular}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With independent active constraints, the KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the reduced Hessian is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\text{ is nonsingular}\iff Z^{\mathsf T}QZ\text{ is nonsingular}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Curvature Characterization of KKT Singularity
Curvature-Induced KKT Ill-Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nearly flat feasible direction supplies an upper bound on the KKT smallest singular value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[K=\begin{bmatrix}Q&J^\top\\J&0\end{bmatrix}\]
with \(Q=Q^\top\). If there is a unit feasible direction \(d\) satisfying \(Jd=0\) and \(\lVert Qd\rVert_2\le\delta\), then
\[K\begin{bmatrix}d\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}Qd\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \sigma_{\min}(K)\le\delta.\]
Thus nearly vanishing curvature along a constraint-tangent direction forces the KKT matrix to have a small singular value. If \(Qd=0\), the KKT matrix is exactly singular. The converse need not hold because constraint dependence or scaling can also cause KKT ill-conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible unit direction with nearly zero curvature forces a small singular value in the active-set KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\min}(K)\le\delta\).

notation.meaning: unit direction tangent to the active constraints

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct singular-value bound from a nearly null feasible-curvature direction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The test-vector bound on the smallest singular value is correct and the property kind fits the consequence leaf, but no supporting source is cited.

children.title: Poor Numerical Scaling
children.top_down_role: Large coefficient-magnitude disparities across objective or constraint data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Tests Are Not Row-Scale Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of equivalent equation scaling on untransformed absolute residual tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Ax=b\) and \(SAx=Sb\) be equivalent equality systems with nonsingular diagonal \(S\). Their residuals satisfy \(\widehat r=S(Ax-b)\). Therefore an absolute test \(\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\) is generally not invariant under row scaling: for \(S=\alpha I\), the reported residual is multiplied by \(|\alpha|\). Consistently transformed or scale-normalized tests are required for invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent row scaling preserves feasibility but can arbitrarily change an unnormalized absolute residual and its stopping decision.
assumptions_latex: The stopping tolerance is not transformed with the row scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat r=Sr,\qquad \lVert\widehat r\rVert_2\text{ can differ arbitrarily from }\lVert r\rVert_2\text{ while the feasible set is unchanged}.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Tests Are Not Row-Scale Invariant
Poor Numerical Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-dependent row and column norm imbalance in a QP linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\ne0\) be a QP coefficient matrix, such as a constraint or KKT matrix, after units and variable conventions have been fixed. For a threshold \(\tau>1\), define
\[\rho_r(M)=\frac{\max_{i:\lVert M_{i:}\rVert_2>0}\lVert M_{i:}\rVert_2}{\min_{i:\lVert M_{i:}\rVert_2>0}\lVert M_{i:}\rVert_2},\qquad
\rho_c(M)=\frac{\max_{j:\lVert M_{:j}\rVert_2>0}\lVert M_{:j}\rVert_2}{\min_{j:\lVert M_{:j}\rVert_2>0}\lVert M_{:j}\rVert_2}.\]
The representation is poorly scaled at threshold \(\tau\) when \(\max\{\rho_r(M),\rho_c(M)\}\ge\tau\). This diagnoses coefficient-scale disparity, not intrinsic mathematical ill-posedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A QP representation is poorly scaled when its nonzero row or column norms span a prescribed large ratio under fixed units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\rho_r(M),\rho_c(M)\}\ge\tau\).

notation.meaning: QP coefficient or KKT matrix under fixed units
ratio of largest to smallest nonzero row norm
ratio of largest to smallest nonzero column norm

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional norm-spread diagnostic for matrix scaling
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The row-and-column norm-spread diagnostic is well defined and explicitly representation-dependent, but it is a chosen scaling convention with no cited authority.

children.title: Unit Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Incompatible physical, financial, or normalized units across model components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact transformation of equality rows and their multipliers under changes of constraint units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the equality-constrained QP with Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)\), let \(S\) be nonsingular diagonal and express the same equations as \(S(Ax-b)=0\). The feasible set is unchanged. If \(\widehat\lambda\) multiplies the scaled equations, stationarity is preserved exactly when \[\lambda=S^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda,\qquad\widehat\lambda=S^{-\mathsf T}\lambda.\] Thus multiplier magnitudes depend on equation units even though the primal problem does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing equality units preserves the feasible set but inversely rescales the associated multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:Ax=b\}=\{x:SAx=Sb\},\qquad \widehat\lambda=S^{-\mathsf T}\lambda.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Unit Conversion and Multiplier Transformation
Unit Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation of QP data under unequal changes of variable units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the QP
\[\min_x\ \tfrac12x^\top Qx+c^\top x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\]
let \(x=Ds\), where \(D\) is a nonsingular diagonal matrix encoding changes of variable units. The equivalent problem in \(s\) has data
\[Q_s=D^\top QD,\qquad c_s=D^\top c,\qquad A_s=AD.\]
Unit imbalance is present when the scale spread \(\max_i|D_{ii}|/\min_i|D_{ii}|\) is large. Although \(x=Ds\) bijectively preserves feasible points and objective values, it can create large coefficient disparities and substantially alter numerical condition measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal variable-unit changes transform QP coefficients by diagonal scaling; a large scale spread can degrade numerical scaling without changing the exact problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s=D^\top QD\), \(c_s=D^\top c\), and \(A_s=AD\), with \(x=Ds\) preserving exact equivalence.

notation.meaning: variable expressed in the new units

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard diagonal change-of-variables formula for quadratic programs
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal change-of-variables formulas and exact-equivalence claim are correct, and representation fits the leaf; however, the characterization of scale spread as large is uncited and lacks a specified threshold.

children.title: Scale-Induced Conditioning Loss
children.top_down_role: Conditioning deterioration caused by unresolved magnitude or unit disparities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General upper bound for conditioning degradation caused by variable scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and nonsingular diagonal \(D\), \[\lambda_{\min}(Q)\sigma_{\min}(D)^2\le\lambda_{\min}(D^{\mathsf T}QD)\le\lambda_{\max}(D^{\mathsf T}QD)\le\lambda_{\max}(Q)\sigma_{\max}(D)^2.\] Consequently, \[\kappa_2(D^{\mathsf T}QD)\le\kappa_2(Q)\kappa_2(D)^2.\] The squared dependence is attained for \(Q=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal variable scaling can worsen Hessian conditioning by the square of the scaling matrix's condition number, and this dependence is sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_2(D^{\mathsf T}QD)\le\kappa_2(Q)\kappa_2(D)^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Bound under Diagonal Congruence

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2(D^{\mathsf T}QD)\) can be arbitrarily larger than \(\kappa_2(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal variable scaling of a positive-definite QP Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the change of variables \(x=Dz\), the quadratic Hessian \(Q\) becomes \(\widehat Q=D^{\mathsf T}QD\). This congruence preserves positive definiteness but need not preserve conditioning. In particular, for \(Q=I_n\) and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,t)\) with \(t\geq 1\), one has \(\kappa_2(Q)=1\) while \(\kappa_2(\widehat Q)=t^2\). Hence scale disparity alone can produce arbitrarily severe conditioning loss in an otherwise perfectly conditioned convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal rescaling preserves convexity but can make a perfectly conditioned Hessian arbitrarily ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Induced Conditioning Loss

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling example is mathematically correct and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but no inspectable numerical-linear-algebra source is cited.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact positive-definiteness and singularity boundary for weighted normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(H\succ0\) and arbitrary \(A\), \[y^{\mathsf T}AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}y=\lVert H^{-1/2}A^{\mathsf T}y\rVert_2^2.\] Hence \(AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\succeq0\), its kernel is \(\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\), and it is positive definite exactly when \(A\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted normal equations are positive definite exactly under full row rank; their kernel is the left nullspace of the constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker(AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})=\ker(A^{\mathsf T}),\qquad AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\succ0\iff\operatorname{rank}A=m.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Loss Boundary for Normal Equations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning bounds for the equality-QP Schur complement with a positive-definite Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, \(H\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), and \(N=AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\). Then \[\frac{\sigma_{\min}(A)^2}{\lambda_{\max}(H)}\le\lambda_{\min}(N)\le\lambda_{\max}(N)\le\frac{\sigma_{\max}(A)^2}{\lambda_{\min}(H)}.\] Consequently \(\kappa_2(N)\le\kappa_2(H)\kappa_2(A)^2\), where the rectangular condition number of \(A\) uses its largest and smallest nonzero singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weighted normal-equation condition number is at most the Hessian condition number times the squared rectangular condition number of the constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_2(AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T})\le\kappa_2(H)\kappa_2(A)^2.

notation.meaning: smallest nonzero singular value of A

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Normal-Equation Spectral Bounds

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), and for \(H=I_n\), \(\kappa_2(AA^{\mathsf T})=\kappa_2(A)^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning of equality-constrained QP normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Eliminating the primal step from a KKT system with Hessian \(H\) produces the normal-equation matrix \(N=AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\), which is positive definite under the stated assumptions. In the unweighted case \(H=I_n\), the nonzero eigenvalues of \(N=AA^{\mathsf T}\) are the squared singular values of \(A\). Consequently, \(\kappa_2(N)=\kappa_2(A)^2\). Thus forming normal equations can square constraint-Jacobian ill-conditioning even when the primal Hessian is perfectly conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal equations are positive definite under full row rank, but in the unweighted case they square the constraint matrix's condition number.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Equation Conditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-equation claim is correct when the rectangular condition number of A uses its nonzero singular values, but that convention and an authoritative locator are missing.

children.title: Sparse Factorization Fill-In
children.top_down_role: Growth of intermediate factor density despite sparse model data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp example showing that sparse input alone does not ensure sparse factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the star on \(n\) vertices. Eliminating its center first joins its \(n-1\) leaves into a clique and creates \(\binom{n-1}{2}\) fill edges, although \(G\) initially has only \(n-1\) edges. Eliminating all leaves before the center creates no fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A star graph produces quadratic fill if its center is eliminated first, but no fill if its leaves are eliminated first.
assumptions_latex: The matrix has the star as its structural graph and admits the stated symbolic elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |F_{\mathrm{center\ first}}|=\binom{n-1}{2},\qquad |F_{\mathrm{leaves\ first}}|=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Star with Quadratic Fill

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph-theoretic boundary for fill-free sparse Cholesky elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\) have undirected structural sparsity graph \(G\), and let \(\pi\) be a symmetric elimination ordering. Symbolic Cholesky elimination in order \(\pi\) creates no fill if and only if the later neighbors of every eliminated vertex form a clique. Thus \(G\) admits a zero-fill ordering if and only if \(G\) is chordal, and its zero-fill orderings are precisely its perfect elimination orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordering is fill-free exactly when it is a perfect elimination ordering; such an ordering exists exactly for chordal graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is the structural sparsity graph of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi\text{ creates no fill}\iff\pi\text{ is a perfect elimination ordering},\qquad \exists\pi\text{ with no fill}\iff G\text{ is chordal}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Fill Characterization by Perfect Elimination

assumptions_latex: A symmetric elimination ordering \(\pi\) is fixed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating a vertex joins all its remaining neighbors, and each newly created edge represents structural fill in the Cholesky factor.

notation.meaning: Cholesky factor of the permuted matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural fill during sparse Cholesky factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the undirected sparsity graph of \(M\) contain an edge \(\{i,j\}\) exactly when \(i\neq j\) and \(M_{ij}\neq0\). When a vertex is eliminated according to \(\pi\), all of its neighbors that remain uneliminated are joined into a clique. An edge introduced by this operation that was absent from the original graph is a fill edge and corresponds, barring numerical cancellation, to a structurally nonzero entry of \(L\) absent from the corresponding triangle of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse elimination connects every pair of remaining neighbors; the new graph edges become structural nonzeros in the factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Factorization Fill-In

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elimination-graph description and numerical-cancellation qualification are appropriate, but the structural-fill correspondence requires a sparse-factorization citation.

children.title: Loss of Block Structure
children.top_down_role: Destruction of separable, bordered, staged, or repeated-block organization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition for the displayed affine-constrained QP representation to separate into independent variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed partition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\), the displayed QP representation separates into independent block subproblems if, after row permutation, \[H=\operatorname{diag}(H_1,\ldots,H_p),\quad c=(c_1,\ldots,c_p),\quad A=\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\ldots,A_p),\quad b=(b_1,\ldots,b_p).\] Equivalently, every displayed objective term and constraint row involves variables from only one block. A nonzero cross-Hessian block or a displayed constraint row incident to multiple blocks destroys this visible decomposition, although equivalent row operations, repartitioning, or reformulation can sometimes recover another decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A displayed QP separates by a fixed block partition when its objective and every represented constraint row respect that partition.
assumptions_latex: A fixed partition of variables is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the displayed compatible block structure, the feasible set is a Cartesian product and the objective is a sum of block objectives.
review_flags: criterion is representation-relative; equivalent row operations or reformulations may reveal a different decomposition
knowledge_statements.title: Visible Independent Block-Decomposition Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Coordinate Change Can Destroy Visible Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-dependent loss of block-diagonal structure without changing the underlying optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\) and \(x=Ty\), where \[T=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}.\] Then \[T^{\mathsf T}HT=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix},\] so the transformed quadratic has a cross term despite being equivalent to the original diagonal quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense rotation can erase visible block separability while preserving mathematical equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The displayed Hessian and orthogonal transformation are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is diagonal, but \(T^{\mathsf T}HT\) is not block diagonal for the scalar partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Coordinate Change Can Destroy Visible Blocks
Loss of Block Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block coupling created by QP Schur-complement elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Although the primal Hessian \(H\) is block diagonal, eliminating primal variables produces \(S=AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\). For constraint row groups \(r\) and \(s\), its block is \(S_{rs}=\sum_{i=1}^p A_{ri}H_i^{-1}A_{si}^{\mathsf T}\). Consequently, whenever this complete sum is nonzero for some \(r\neq s\), the reduced system couples those row groups and cannot be factored as independent row-group subproblems. A variable block participating in both groups can create such coupling, although cancellation among summands may prevent it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating block-separable primal variables can create nonzero off-diagonal Schur blocks that couple constraint groups and prevent independent block solves; contributions from different variable blocks can also cancel.
assumptions_latex: The constraint matrix is partitioned compatibly into blocks \(A_{ri}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(S_{rs}=\sum_{i=1}^p A_{ri}H_i^{-1}A_{si}^{\mathsf T}\neq0\) for some \(r\neq s\), then the corresponding row groups are coupled in the reduced system.

notation.meaning: constraint block for row group r and variable group i

children.title: Ordering-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Memory or runtime sensitivity to variable ordering, constraint ordering, or elimination choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit sparsity pattern exhibiting linear versus quadratic factor storage solely from different elimination orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a symmetric positive-definite matrix whose undirected sparsity graph is a star with one center and \(n-1\) leaves. Eliminating all leaves before the center creates no fill and gives \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=2n-1\). Eliminating the center first makes all leaves pairwise adjacent, so the remaining filled graph is a clique and \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=n(n+1)/2\). Under scalar outer-product Cholesky, the corresponding work is respectively \(\Theta(n)\) and \(\Theta(n^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A star pattern has linear factor complexity under leaf-first elimination but dense-factor complexity under center-first elimination.
assumptions_latex: The matrix is symmetric positive definite.
Its structural graph is a star.
Scalar Cholesky uses the stated elimination order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=2n-1\) leaf-first, but \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=n(n+1)/2\) center-first.
knowledge_statements.title: Star-Graph Ordering Separation

assumptions_latex: \(M\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) is factored by scalar sparse Cholesky elimination
\(d_k\) counts the uneliminated neighbors of the kth eliminated vertex after fill
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=n+\sum_k d_k\) and the arithmetic work is \(\Theta(\sum_k(d_k+1)^2)\), both ordering-dependent.

notation.meaning: filled elimination degree at step k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering-dependent storage and arithmetic for scalar sparse Cholesky.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed ordering \(\pi\), the column generated at elimination step \(k\) has \(d_k+1\) structural entries. Hence the factor storage is \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=n+\sum_{k=1}^n d_k\), and the usual outer-product Cholesky implementation performs \(\Theta(\sum_{k=1}^n(d_k+1)^2)\) arithmetic operations. Because each elimination changes the graph seen by later steps, different orderings can produce different sequences \((d_k)\), ranging from sparse factors to nearly dense factors for the same matrix sparsity pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse Cholesky storage and work depend on filled elimination degrees, which can change drastically with the ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Sensitive Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and ordering-dependent formulas are suitable, but the implementation-dependent arithmetic bound requires a precise sparse-Cholesky cost reference.

children.title: Penalty Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Penalty choices that distort intended priorities, violations, or soft-constraint costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalty weights lack invariant meaning unless the normalization of the penalized residual is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing \(r(x)=0\) by \(\frac{\rho}{2}r(x)^2\) is not invariant under an equivalent rescaling. Writing the constraint as \(\alpha r(x)=0\), where \(\alpha\ne0\), produces \(\frac{\rho}{2}(\alpha r(x))^2=\frac{\rho\alpha^2}{2}r(x)^2\). Retaining the same numerical \(\rho\) therefore changes the effective penalty weight and can change the penalized optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling an equality changes the effective quadratic-penalty weight, so an unadjusted penalty parameter can change the solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\rho}{2}(\alpha r(x))^2=\frac{\rho\alpha^2}{2}r(x)^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Scaling Dependence of Quadratic Penalties

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite quadratic penalty need not enforce the intended equality constraint exactly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite quadratic penalties for equality-constrained convex QPs.

source_refs.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the constrained convex QP \(\min_x \tfrac12(x-1)^2\) subject to \(x=0\). Replacing the equality by a quadratic penalty gives \(\min_x \tfrac12(x-1)^2+\tfrac{\rho}{2}x^2\), whose unique minimizer is \(x_\rho=(1+\rho)^{-1}\). Thus \(x_\rho\neq0\) for every finite \(\rho\), although \(x_\rho\to0\) as \(\rho\to\infty\). Treating a finite quadratic penalty as exact therefore misspecifies the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite quadratic penalty can leave a nonzero constraint violation even in a one-dimensional strictly convex QP.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Misspecification

source_witnesses.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and fits the leaf, but the chapter-level locator is not sufficiently specific and its nonquadratic-penalty title does not clearly support the quadratic-penalty claim.

children.title: Regularization Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Regularization choices that impose unsuitable shrinkage, smoothing, or curvature.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing ridge regularization can impose a minimum-norm selection absent from the original QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\), \(c\in\operatorname{range}(Q)\), and \(S=\arg\min_x\{\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\}\). For \(\lambda>0\), the ridge-regularized problem has the unique minimizer \(x_\lambda=-(Q+\lambda I)^{-1}c\). As \(\lambda\downarrow0\), \(x_\lambda\to-Q^\dagger c\), the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm member of \(S\). Thus vanishing regularization still imposes a selection rule when the original minimizer is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing ridge regularization selects the minimum-norm member of a nonunique solution set and can impose an unintended preference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\lambda\downarrow0}x_\lambda=-Q^\dagger c=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S}\|x\|_2.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Selects Among Unregularized Minimizers

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\lambda=-(Q+\lambda I)^{-1}c\) generally differs from the unregularized minimizer \(x_0=-Q^{-1}c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution bias caused by ridge regularization in a convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unregularized QP \(\min_x \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x\) has unique minimizer \(x_0=-Q^{-1}c\). Adding ridge regularization produces \(\min_x \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+c^{\mathsf T}x+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert x\rVert_2^2\), with minimizer \(x_\lambda=-(Q+\lambda I)^{-1}c\). Unless the induced displacement vanishes, \(x_\lambda\neq x_0\). Consequently, selecting \(\lambda\) solely for numerical conditioning changes the modeled optimizer and introduces regularization bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive ridge regularization improves curvature but generally moves the optimizer, so a numerically convenient parameter can bias the model.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ridge-induced optimizer displacement is correct and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but no regularization-bias source is supplied.

children.title: Penalty-Regularization Tradeoff Failures
children.top_down_role: Regimes where competing coefficient choices produce unintended model behavior.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimizer \(x_{\rho,\lambda}=\rho/(\rho+\lambda)\) has violation \(\lambda/(\rho+\lambda)\), exposing competing penalty and regularization effects.
review_flags: regularization aspect needs a more specific locator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict between feasibility penalties and shrinkage regularization.

source_refs.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the intended hard constraint \(x=1\), consider the unconstrained model \(\min_x \tfrac{\rho}{2}(x-1)^2+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}x^2\). Its unique minimizer is \(x_{\rho,\lambda}=\rho/(\rho+\lambda)\), so the constraint violation is \(1-x_{\rho,\lambda}=\lambda/(\rho+\lambda)\). Increasing \(\rho\) improves feasibility, whereas increasing \(\lambda\) strengthens shrinkage toward zero and worsens feasibility. Parameter choices made independently can therefore defeat either the constraint surrogate or the regularization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty and ridge parameters can pull the solution in opposing directions, so independently chosen values can undermine feasibility or shrinkage goals.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Regularization Tradeoff Failures

source_witnesses.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar tradeoff calculation is correct, but the cited chapter-level penalty locator does not specifically support the ridge-regularization side of the claim.

children.title: Surrogate-Loss Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Quadratic surrogate choices that poorly reflect the intended prediction or decision loss.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decision Consistency of a Surrogate Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population-level consistency of a quadratic surrogate for a fixed target loss under one data law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty decision set \(X\), surrogate risk \(S\), and target risk \(R\), with relevant minima attained, the surrogate is decision-consistent when \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}S(x)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}R(x).\] Surrogate-loss mismatch occurs when this containment fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every surrogate-risk optimizer must also minimize target risk; otherwise the surrogate loss is mismatched.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(R\) are defined on the same nonempty decision set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mismatch is equivalent to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_XS\nsubseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_XR\).
knowledge_statements.title: Decision Consistency of a Surrogate Loss

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition under which surrogate optimization accuracy controls target-risk accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S^*=\inf_XS\) and \(R^*=\inf_XR\). Suppose a nondecreasing function \(\delta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\), with \(\delta(0)=0\) and \(\delta(t)>0\) for every \(t>0\), satisfies \[S(x)-S^*\ge\delta\bigl(R(x)-R^*\bigr)\quad\text{for all }x\in X.\] Then any sequence satisfying \(S(x_k)\to S^*\) also satisfies \(R(x_k)\to R^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive calibration function transfers vanishing surrogate regret into vanishing target regret.
assumptions_latex: The displayed calibration inequality holds on \(X\).
\(\delta\) is nondecreasing, vanishes at zero, and is positive away from zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(x_k)\to S^*\Longrightarrow R(x_k)\to R^*\).

notation.meaning: optimal surrogate and target risk values

knowledge_statements.title: Calibration Transfer of Surrogate Convergence

assumptions_latex: \(Y\) equals \(0\) with probability \(0.9\) and \(10\) with probability \(0.1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic-surrogate minimizer is \(1\), whereas the absolute-risk minimizer is \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic surrogate used for an absolute-error target risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constant predictions \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), the quadratic surrogate risk \(S(x)=\mathbb{E}(x-Y)^2\) is minimized uniquely at \(x=\mathbb{E}Y=1\). The target absolute-error risk \(R(x)=\mathbb{E}|x-Y|\) is minimized at any median of \(Y\), here uniquely at \(x=0\). Therefore the convex quadratic surrogate selects a decision that is not target-risk optimal. Convexity and tractability of the QP do not by themselves establish alignment with the intended loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a skewed two-point distribution, squared loss selects the mean while absolute loss selects the median, producing different optimal decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate-Loss Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mean-versus-median counterexample is correct and the counterexample kind fits the leaf, but no statistical-decision source is cited.

children.title: Risk-Model Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Quadratic risk representations that omit relevant exposures, asymmetries, or tail behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second Moments Do Not Determine Tail-Sensitive Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary of variance-only quadratic risk representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_a\) equal \(-1\) and \(1\) with probabilities \(1/2,1/2\), and let \(L_b\) equal \(-2,0,2\) with probabilities \(1/8,3/4,1/8\). Then \[\mathbb EL_a=\mathbb EL_b=0,\qquad \mathbb EL_a^2=\mathbb EL_b^2=1,\] but \[\mathbb EL_a^4=1\neq4=\mathbb EL_b^4.\] Thus a mean-variance model cannot distinguish these losses although a fourth-moment criterion does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two losses can have identical means and variances but different fourth moments, so variance-only risk can omit tail-sensitive information.
assumptions_latex: \(L_a\) and \(L_b\) have the displayed discrete distributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The losses have equal first and second moments but unequal fourth moments.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Moments Do Not Determine Tail-Sensitive Risk

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Misspecification of the risk functional while the decision domain and loss interpretation remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_0\) be modeled risk and \(R_1\) true risk on a common nonempty decision set \(X\), with both minima attained. The model is decision-consistent when \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}R_0(x)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}R_1(x).\] Risk-model mismatch occurs when this containment fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every modeled-risk optimizer must be truly risk-optimal; failure of this containment is risk-model mismatch.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Risk-model mismatch is equivalent to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_XR_0\nsubseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_XR_1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Modeled-versus-True Risk Mismatch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision stability under a uniform discrepancy between modeled and true risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\sup_{x\in X}|R_0(x)-R_1(x)|\le\varepsilon\) and \(x_0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_X R_0\), then \[0\le R_1(x_0)-\inf_{x\in X}R_1(x)\le2\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform risk-model error of at most epsilon limits the true-risk regret of a modeled optimizer to twice epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1(x_0)-\inf_XR_1\le2\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Risk-Error Regret Bound

assumptions_latex: The modeled law has mean \(0\), while the true law has mean \(1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The modeled squared-risk optimizer is \(0\), while the true squared-risk optimizer is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional mismatch in a quadratic expected-risk model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\) be a modeled distribution satisfying \(\mathbb{E}_{P_0}Y=0\), and let the true distribution \(P_1\) satisfy \(\mathbb{E}_{P_1}Y=1\), with both second moments finite. The modeled QP minimizes \(R_0(x)=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}(x-Y)^2\) and therefore selects \(x_0=0\). Actual squared risk is \(R_1(x)=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}(x-Y)^2\), whose unique minimizer is \(x_1=1\). Thus an exact solution of the modeled QP can be suboptimal under the true risk model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A wrong distributional mean makes the exact modeled least-squares optimizer differ from the true risk optimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Model Mismatch

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-second-moment assumptions suffice and the modeled-versus-true optimizer comparison is correct, but an inspectable statistical-risk source is absent.

children.title: Objective-to-Risk Alignment Failures
children.top_down_role: Misalignment between optimized surrogate objectives and the risk criteria used for evaluation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-level agreement between an optimized QP objective and the intended risk, without requiring preservation of every pairwise ranking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), and suppose \(q,R:X\to\mathbb R\) attain their minima. The objective \(q\) is optimal-set aligned with \(R\) when \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}q(x)\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}R(x).\] Alignment fails exactly when some \(x_q\in\operatorname*{argmin}_X q\) satisfies \[R(x_q)>\min_{x\in X}R(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every QP optimizer must also be risk-optimal; a QP optimizer with positive target-risk regret certifies failure.
assumptions_latex: Both \(q\) and \(R\) attain their minima on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is aligned with \(R\) if and only if \(\operatorname*{argmin}_Xq\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_XR\).
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Set Objective-to-Risk Alignment

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair \(x,y\in X\) with \(q(x)<q(y)\) and \(R(x)>R(y)\) certifies objective-to-risk misalignment.
review_flags: source required for this local alignment criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise certificate of disagreement between a QP objective and risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Objective-to-risk order alignment requires that, for all \(x,y\in X\), strict improvement in the modeled objective not reverse the intended risk ordering. Accordingly, any pair satisfying \(q(x)<q(y)\) and \(R(x)>R(y)\) is a directly checkable certificate of alignment failure. If such a pair includes a QP minimizer \(x\) and some comparator \(y\), then optimizing \(q\) selects a decision with strictly larger intended risk than \(y\), irrespective of solver accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision pair whose quadratic-objective ranking reverses its risk ranking certifies objective-to-risk misalignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-to-Risk Alignment Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reversed-ranking pair is a valid certificate for the stated order-alignment criterion, and the certificate kind fits the leaf, but the criterion has no cited source.

assumptions_latex: The admissible set for \(b\) contains distinct values \(b_1\neq b_2\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The robust hard-feasibility set \(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{x:x=b\}\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility caused by imposing uncertain requirements as universal equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a model requires one decision \(x\) to satisfy \(x=b\) for every admissible \(b\in B\). If \(b_1,b_2\in B\) and \(b_1\neq b_2\), then no \(x\) can satisfy both \(x=b_1\) and \(x=b_2\). Hence \(\bigcap_{b\in B}\{x:x=b\}=\varnothing\). Encoding uncertain or mutually inconsistent requirements as simultaneous hard constraints can therefore make a convex QP infeasible even though each scenario-specific QP is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring one decision to equal every value of a non-singleton uncertain parameter makes the robust QP infeasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Constraint Overcommitment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The non-singleton uncertain-equality example correctly establishes robust infeasibility and fits a failure boundary, but no robust-optimization source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed general affine infeasibility certificate; canonically owned by the dedicated primal-infeasible-status topic rather than this modeling leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the hard affine system \(Ax=b,\;Gx\le h\), infeasibility is equivalent to the existence of \(y\) and \(z\ge0\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas multiplier pair certifies infeasibility of a mixed affine system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:Ax=b,\;Gx\le h\}=\varnothing\iff\exists(y,z):z\ge0,\;A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0,\;b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Certificate of Hard-Constraint Overcommitment

children.title: Solver-Tolerance Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of reported feasibility, optimality, or termination on numerical tolerance choices.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolute Residual Tests Depend on Constraint Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent affine formulations can receive different classifications under an unnormalized absolute tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a^{\mathsf T}x=b\), let \(r(x)=|a^{\mathsf T}x-b|\). The equivalent equality \(\alpha a^{\mathsf T}x=\alpha b\), \(\alpha\ne0\), has residual \(r_\alpha(x)=|\alpha|r(x)\). Hence \(r_\alpha(x)\le\varepsilon\) is equivalent to \(r(x)\le\varepsilon/|\alpha|\), not generally to \(r(x)\le\varepsilon\). An unnormalized absolute tolerance can therefore change acceptance under an equivalent reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling an equivalent constraint changes the effective absolute tolerance and can change whether a fixed point is accepted.
assumptions_latex: Acceptance uses an unnormalized absolute residual
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_\alpha(x)=|\alpha|r(x),\qquad r_\alpha(x)\le\varepsilon\iff r(x)\le\varepsilon/|\alpha|.
review_flags: normalized or relative residual conventions may avoid this scaling effect
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Residual Tests Depend on Constraint Scaling
Solver-Tolerance Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of residual-based acceptance on absolute solver tolerances for a convex quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the convex QP 
\[\min_x \tfrac12 x^\top Qx+c^\top x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\;Gx\le h,\qquad Q\succeq0.\]
For a candidate primal-dual triple \((x,y,z)\) with \(z\ge0\), define \(R=\max\{\lVert Ax-b\rVert_\infty,\lVert(Gx-h)_+\rVert_\infty,\lVert Qx+c+A^\top y+G^\top z\rVert_\infty,\lVert z\odot(Gx-h)\rVert_\infty\}\). If acceptance means \(R\le\varepsilon\), then the acceptance sets are nested: \(0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\) implies \(\{R\le\varepsilon_1\}\subseteq\{R\le\varepsilon_2\}\). Whenever \(\varepsilon_1<R\le\varepsilon_2\), the same computed triple fails the tighter test and passes the looser test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-based acceptance is monotone in the tolerance, and a fixed computed solution changes classification whenever its residual lies between two tested tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Acceptance uses the displayed absolute infinity-norm residual test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_1<R\le\varepsilon_2\Longrightarrow (R\nleq\varepsilon_1\ \text{and}\ R\le\varepsilon_2)\).

notation.meaning: maximum primal-feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity residual
componentwise positive part of a vector

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically correct for the explicitly defined residual test, matches the leaf, and uses an appropriate content kind. However, it has no citation, and the particular residual and acceptance convention is solver-dependent; a source with a specific section, page, or solver-tolerance definition is required.

children.title: Solver-Status Misinterpretation
children.top_down_role: Incorrect conclusions drawn from approximate, limited, ambiguous, or failure-status reports.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noncertifying Termination Does Not Determine Mathematical Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between operational termination reports and mathematical QP statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A termination report caused only by an iteration limit, time limit, user interruption, or numerical failure establishes neither primal infeasibility nor unboundedness nor optimality unless the returned data also satisfy a corresponding mathematical certificate. Absence of a certified solution is not a certificate that no solution exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limit or failure status alone proves neither optimality nor infeasibility; a corresponding certificate must be checked.
assumptions_latex: The termination reason supplies no valid optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness certificate
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{noncertifying termination}\not\Rightarrow\text{optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness}.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncertifying Termination Does Not Determine Mathematical Status
Solver-Status Misinterpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A residual-qualified solver status does not imply exact feasibility or exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon\) and consider the one-dimensional convex QP
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R} x^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\ge\delta.\]
At \(x=0\), the objective gradient is zero and the constraint violation is \(\delta\). Hence a solver whose approximate-feasibility rule accepts violations at most \(\varepsilon\) may classify \(x=0\) as approximately feasible and stationary. Nevertheless, \(x=0\) is not feasible for the mathematical QP, whose unique optimizer is \(x^\star=\delta\). Thus interpreting a tolerance-qualified status such as “solved” as a claim of exact feasibility and exact optimality is invalid without checking the solver’s residual definitions and tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point may satisfy a solver’s approximate residual tests yet be infeasible and nonoptimal for the exact convex QP.
assumptions_latex: The solver accepts scalar constraint violation not exceeding \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=0\) may pass the approximate test, but \(0<\delta\) implies \(x=0\) is exactly infeasible and \(x^\star=\delta\).

notation.meaning: positive displacement of the exact feasible region from zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar counterexample is correct and appropriately classified: x=0 can pass the stated approximate feasibility test while remaining exactly infeasible, and the exact optimizer is x*=delta. The connection from these residual facts to a status such as “solved” depends on documented solver semantics, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Tolerance-Driven Status Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Cases where tolerance settings blur distinctions among solved, inaccurate, infeasible, or indeterminate outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Driven Status Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp feasibility-tolerance boundary for contradictory scalar linear constraints embedded in a convex QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\delta>0\), consider the convex QP
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R} 0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\le0,\;-x\le-\delta.\]
The exact feasible set is empty. Define the maximum violation \(V(x)=\max\{(x)_+,(-x+\delta)_+\}\). Its minimum is \(\min_xV(x)=\delta/2\), attained at \(x=\delta/2\). Consequently, an approximate-feasibility test \(V(x)\le\varepsilon\) has an accepted point exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge\delta/2\), although the QP remains exactly infeasible. Near this threshold, changing only the feasibility tolerance can therefore support either rejection of every candidate or acceptance of an approximately feasible candidate, making an unqualified status semantically ambiguous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contradictory constraints admit an approximately feasible point exactly when tolerance reaches half their separation, despite exact infeasibility at every tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Approximate feasibility is defined by \(V(x)\le\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:V(x)\le\varepsilon\}\ne\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow\varepsilon\ge\delta/2\), while the exact feasible set is empty.

notation.meaning: maximum componentwise violation of the two inequalities
separation between the contradictory constraint boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sharp threshold min_x V(x)=delta/2 is correct, the exact feasible set is empty, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. Nevertheless, the claimed status ambiguity depends on how a solver maps approximate feasibility to statuses, and the record supplies no citation with a specific locator supporting that interpretation.
